Festivities concluded later that evening with a ball in the Salón Imperial. The organizers held a raffle with prizes including famous works of art, TV sets, sound systems and ten new cars.

Meanwhile the doctors and interns still striking saw their movement collapsing around them. The few who dared picket in the streets were harrassed by police and onlookers. Others tried returning to work only to discover they'd been fired and blacklisted. Their leaders were either desperately trying to flee the country or already behind bars.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.3.a: Gone, and soon to be forgotten.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.3.tt: The crackdown on the £GFX_DoctorsStrike_doctors AMM and the £GFX_DoctorsStrike_interns AMMRI has led to the disbanding of the unions and the victory of Ordaz in the £GFX_DoctorsStrike_doctors Doctor's Strike!
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.4.desc:
The clamor in the hotel conference room was deafening. Only a few people sat at the tables. Most, including Lupita, were on their feet, commiserating about their slim chances of catching the president's ear. Lupita was happy to be here, though she couldn't help but wish her first visit to the Federal District had come under better circumstances. She had been elected by the Saltillo chapter to represent them at a national meeting of the AMMRI, and didn't have the time or money for sightseeing.

Lupita was feeling horribly overwhelmed by all the commotion when she was waved into a circle of interns on the edge of the crowd. There, a handsome young man was ranting about their parent organization, the AMM. He was almost shouting just to be heard over the din.

“All I'm saying is that if the doctors really cared about us, they wouldn't have waited two months to go on strike. Ordaz will listen to whatever it is they want to say and he'll shut them down just like he did last time.” Lupita nodded along with the rest of the group.

“Then why the hell should we follow their orders?” She was surprised to hear herself speak, but continued when she saw the other interns were listening intently. “Just because they'll back down to save their careers doesn't mean we have to stop too. We'll get out of the streets when Ordaz gives in.” Cheers went up around the circle.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.4.a: Their strike would go on, with or without the AMM.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.5.desc:
The Saltillo chapter of the AMMRI filled the street outside of the civil hospital, chanting slogans and waving signs. Ordaz had refused to bend to their demands, but the R/Is were sure another round of strikes would bring the president to the negotiating table. It had to.

Somewhere in the distance, sirens spun up to a terrible wail. It was only when police vans came racing down the street that Lupita took notice of the sound. The howling continued as a legion of cops wielding batons filed out of the vehicles and formed into a line, blocking any avenue of escape. Somewhere, a whistle shrieked. The police began to march in lockstep towards the demonstrators.

Already, some of the crowd began to turn and flee. A wave of blue uniforms broke against the mass of protestors. Lupita tried to run, but couldn't squeeze through the densely packed crowd behind her. All she could do was watch as the police thrashed her fellow interns with their truncheons. Another wave of people began to flee as it became clear the police were not interested in making arrests.

Lupita darted for an opening in the thinning crowd behind her when a calloused hand closed around her wrist. Before she could turn to face her captor, a baton slammed into her shoulder. She felt her collarbone break with a dull snap. Lupita screamed. Searing pain radiated from her shattered clavicle. Then the baton struck her in the head. Her legs gave way. All around her were barked orders and screams and the smack of batons against muscle and bone. The baton came down on her skull twice more before she lost consciousness.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.5.a: The last sounds she heard were screams and the roar of sirens.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.6.desc:
Lupita and the rest of the Saltillo chapter of the AMMRI occupied the street outside the civil hospital, shouting slogans in the dry heat. Suddenly, Lupita found her voice drowned by the deep roar of diesel engines. Three humpbacked garbage trucks were rolling down the street towards the crowd. The lumbering vehicles pulled to a stop, corralling the protestors in the street.

The sanitation workers jumped out of the trucks sporting stained canvas coveralls with CTM pins on the collars. Almost immediately they began to heckle the interns.

“Don't want to be stuck in the union with the idiot garbage collectors? You think you're too good for us? Like you give a fuck about anything but your own pay!” Hydraulics whined as the sloping tailgates on the backs of the vehicles opened. The workers reached into the containers and pulled out the city's refuse. Decaying food, glass bottles, and scrap wood became ammunition for their skirmish.

Lupita found herself face to face with one of the sanitation workers, a wiry man with a shaved head. He pulled a bloated, moldy orange from the truck and hurled it at Lupita. It burst open on her face with a smack.

The smell was unbearable. Liquid ran down her face into her eyes and mouth. She spat it out on the tarmac and wiped her face. Half the crowd had already been driven away by the stench. Lupita ducked as a glass bottle soared past her and shattered on the ground. She decided she would be safer at home.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.6.a: The stains would never come out of Lupita's white coat.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.7.desc:
Roberto and Isabel watched the silent green line on the heart monitor waver. With every breath Lupita took, her heart sped up, and the space between the peaks shrunk. Hope flared, if only for a second. It was quickly dashed when their daughter would exhale into the black silicone oxygen mask. The valleys between her heartbeats would grow intraversably vast in the interval between breaths. On and on it went, as Dr. Vallejo listed their daughter's conditions.

“Sinus Bradycardia... Depressed fracture on the parietal bone... Internal hemorrhage...” Roberto and Isabel could only focus on their daughter's bruised and swollen face. The litany of medical terms did not pierce the haze of grief. The only thing in the world that mattered was Lupita's broken body under the white sheet.

“We're just not sure when she'll wake up, if she does at all.” Roberto's impassive mask shattered as quiet sobs wracked his body. Isabel buried her head in her hands. Tears ran down her arms. “If you have any further questions, I'll be-” Suddenly, the door to the hospital room flew open, and a nurse marched in.

“Dr. Vallejo, we need you in room 14. One of the other demonstrators is going into cardiac arrest.” He gave the bereaved parents an apologetic look and followed the nurse out. The sounds of the hospital filtered through the open door. Shoes scuffed on the tile floor. The few remaining interns ran from room to room. Someone shouted for a scalpel. Tortured wails echoed in the hall. The door closed again.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.7.a: Roberto and Isabel cried in each other's arms as the sun set over Saltillo.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.8.desc:
Golden morning light filtered through sheer curtains into Lupita's sparsely furnished bedroom. She was filling a fiberglass suitcase with clothes from a tall pile in the corner. Lupita was going north. Two of her friends who were at the protest outside the hospital had already been arrested and charged with Social Dissolution. She would not be joining them.

Lupita glanced at the train schedule on her nightstand one last time. If there were no delays, she would make it to Eagle Pass before sundown. She hefted the suitcase off the bed and made for the front door. Standing at the entrance, she rifled through her purse to make sure everything was there. Oh no. Her passport was gone. She dropped the suitcase and darted back through the kitchen to her bedroom.

Tears welled in her eyes as she dug through the pile of clothes. It wasn't there. She started pulling drawers on her dresser at random. All empty. She wiped the tears from her eyes, and started checking under furniture. The dresser? Nothing. Nightstand? No. Under the bed? Something glimmered under a discarded blouse. She snatched it up. It was a blue book with an eagle devouring a snake stamped on the cover in gold foil. She hugged the passport to her chest and put it in her bag.

Lupita grabbed her suitcase from its place by the door and stepped outside. It was a beautiful day. Clear blue sky. Quiet and warm. A slight breeze tousled her hair. She had only gone half a block when a blue and white Dodge came roaring down the street. It stopped in front of her with a horrible screech. Her body went numb. The suitcase slipped from her limp fingers and fell to the ground with a thud.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.8.a: She went into the back seat of the police car without a word.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.9.desc:
The judge's papery skin stretched sickeningly over his gaunt face as he spoke. It seemed that at any moment it would slough off to reveal his true form. A smiling devil that delighted in torment? No. Lupita had never seen any expression on the old bastard's face other than a stern glare. The creature on the bench staring down at her was not one capable of empathy, or any emotion other than paternal fury.

“You and your accomplices have spent months conducting inflammatory demonstrations, disturbing public order, and attempting to spread your insurgent labor movement across the nation. For the crime of social dissolution, you will be sentenced to six years in prison.”

The world around Lupita receded away from her. It felt like she was watching the courtroom through binoculars from somewhere in the back of her skull. She wanted to scream or cry or do something, anything. No noise escaped her mouth. She blinked back tears.

Cameras flashed as police men approached the defendant's table. Anger surged in the gallery. The judge slammed the gavel on the bench. The only sound left were sobs from her parents. The policemen shepherded Lupita out of the courtroom.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.9.a: Tears fell from her face, staining the carpet as she left.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.10.desc:
The gathered members of the AMM were abuzz with activity; the allied professionals snuck in side-chatter and mentally prepared comments on the upcoming topic. The debates of the AMM are unlike the halls of power with their politicians and technocrats or the equal yet direct discussions of the unions, with their working-class origins. Instead, the doctors, interns, and medical students reflect the institutions they toiled away so much of their youth in: academia. Their decisions mirror those of the lecture halls; the truth is the path forward. Identical copies of a recent agreement with the President are passed to all the delegates. Many knew this was coming; others flipped through the pages furiously as they studied the information as quickly as possible as if a test was about to be taken.

“Congratulations, gentlemen,” One of the representatives from the 20 de November hospital began. While on paper a mere signature, these words are proof of the efficacy of our tactics and the strength of our movement. Momentum is on our side. If we wish to see further success, we should continue forward in cooperation with the government, no matter our personal feelings on their ideology.“

A group of delegates from Veracruz speak to one another in hushed whispers, drowned out by the general chatter of the room. A man stands up at eye level with the previous speaker. ”I appreciate the desire for high spirits, but I must advise caution. A tantalizing symbolic victory is simply that—symbolic. The PRI machine wishes to quell and diffuse us—a classic tactic. May I suggest further discussion before deciding our next actions?“
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.10.a: There is always time for further discussion.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.11.desc:
Agent Tomás entered the AMM assembly with trepidation. His case officer had selected him for the assignment only a week ago, not long after the DFS got wind of the event, they had been eager to get someone inside the movement to gather info. After a too-short crash course on medical terminology Tomás was sent into the field.

Tomás remained near the back of the crowd, away from the stage. The speakers weren't due to begin for another few minutes. He would use the time to listen to the attendees, and to single out the most radical members.

“First meeting?” A smiling woman in her 40s materialized out of the crowd. Tomás smiled, nodded, and turned his attention back to the crowd. The doctor narrowed her eyes. “I haven't seen you here before. where's your chapter?” She said flatly. People were turning to look at him.

“Chiapas. I'm from a missionary hospital by the coast. There's only a handful of us.” Feedback shrieked from the stage. The speakers were about to begin. Thank God. Tomás hushed the Doctor and feigned rapt attention.

He had two strategies to pick from regarding the AMM. The first was to try to take a more active role. Divide the organization and push for more radical action. The second was to stick to the original mission. Keep his head down and gather information to report back to the DFS. Neither would be easy.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.11.a: Make the AMM do our work for us.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.11.b: Stay the course, stay out of trouble.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.12.desc:
After nearly being outed as a fraud at his first AMM meeting, Tomás knew that the original plan was untenable. When he returned to his case officer, he made his concerns clear. He had no clue how long he could stay undercover, especially since the AMM was an organization of experts in a field where he had only cursory knowledge. A more direct route would be necessary.

The date of the second meeting came. Tomás sat calmly through the reading of the previous minutes and the opening statements. When the chairman opened the floor for motions, Tomás stood.

“We need more radical action.” The room went quiet. “We've been in the streets for months now and nothing has changed. We can't just march passively through the streets waving signs expecting the president to listen! We shouldn't give them the option to ignore us! I move to demand the cessation of all medical services until our demands are met!”

The chairman looked back at him in disbelief. “You're suggesting that not only do we abandon every oath we took as medical practitioners, but we give this administration every excuse to crack down on our movement while we do it? Motion denied.”

Another doctor stood. “I move to expel the doctor from the AMM, effective immediately.” Tomás glanced around. He had overplayed his hand. The vote to expel him was near unanimous.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.12.a: Tomás braced himself for an earful from his handler, and headed back to the office.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.13.desc:
Agent Tomás pushed open the door to the darkened office of the empty warehouse. The few beams of light that permeated the papered-over windows only illuminated a haze of cigarette smoke. Another agent hunched over a tanker desk, staring at an empty tape player.

“You're late,” said agent Víctor, his superior.

“It was a pain in the ass to get this tape out,” Tomás replied. He pulled a small device from his pocket. Roughly rectangular, with two small reels of magnetic tape on the front. A cord led from the machine to a small microphone. “Just put it in the machine, you'll understand,” Tomás replied. Víctor put the reels into the tape player, and pushed play.

“Morning, Leandro.” Tomás identified the voice as the chairman of the AMM. The bug must have been planted somewhere in the AMM's main offices.

“Good morning, Ricardo.” This was the voice of the treasurer. They exchanged pleasantries, and inquired about each other's families for a few minutes. Víctor was starting to get impatient.

“Are we still planning on holding the demonstration at the 20 de November Hospital after the next national meeting?” the chairman rasped. Víctor's eyebrows shot up as he removed a pad and pen from the desk.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.13.a: “Good work, Agent Tomás,” Víctor said with a smile.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.14.desc:
After a long day of leading strikes, medical intern Ferdinand carefully unlocked the front door to his vecindad apartment with heavy eyes. It wasn't much to speak of, but it was his, and it was centrally located on the checkerboard block of Mexico City, so he could get around quickly. As soon as he entered, he placed his bag, coat, and shoes in their designated spot. Ferdinand was only ever a couple of steps from anywhere in his home, so everything had to be in its place for any sense of organization. The divide between the kitchen and living room was more loose suggestion than distinct rooms.

Once he had shed the burdens of the outside world, Ferdinand made a beeline for his functional kitchen. A headache pounded dully against his skull, like being tapped by a rubber mallet. The grueling hours spent on the 20 de November Hospital picket line had taken a toll on his body. He gulped down a glass of water, the cool liquid soothing his parched throat, raw from hours of non-stop talking. Still focused on hydration, Ferdinand reached for his nearby standing lamp, his only light source in the dimly lit room.

The hair on the back of Ferdinand's neck stood up. His lamp wasn't there. With fresh eyes, he looked around his room. The lamp was in another corner. Something was off. He would have remembered moving his lamp. Ferdinand's throat tightened once again, and a flash of heat washed over him as his heart dropped. But that wasn't all. Turning on the light, he scoured his apartment. Furniture has been moved around, the bathroom light is on, and all his family pictures had been set up in a line on his small desk.

Ferdinand's hands shake as he closes his window, which, usually closed to keep in the heat, is wide open and facing a rooftop in the distance. With the initial panic fading, Ferdinand is forced by exhaustion to reach the obvious conclusion: Someone had been in his home. Mustering the strength to sleep, he convinces himself he cannot see the light across the street.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.15.desc:
Ferdinand's hand trembled as he cautiously grasped his apartment's door handle. His once secure haven had been violated just the day before. The harsh realities of life and his principles compelled him to return to the picket line, but the unsettling thought of an unknown intruder invading his personal space lingered. He dared not share his concerns with his comrades, unsure of who he could trust and fearful of being dismissed as delusional. In his other hand, he tightly clutched a switchblade borrowed from a friend, symbolizing his growing unease.

With as much strength as he could muster, Ferdinand swung open the door and saw nothing. He arrived ready for a fight and everything to be rearranged again, but nothing was out of order. He let out a sigh of relief as he searched his small home once again to make sure. He must have been seeing things after all, or perhaps the neighborhood kids were playing a prank on him.

Almost drowned out by the ambient sounds of his apartment, Ferdinand's keen ears picked up a faint, droning whisper. His heart raced, and a shiver ran down his spine as he feared the worst. The rhythmic beat of his ceiling fan guided him to his bedroom, where he found everything in its place. Yet on his bedside desk, his radio was playing music with sounds as small as its 'made in Guangdong' inscription.

Ferdinand turned the dial to his radio slightly until he felt the satisfying click of the off position. He must have left it on when he departed that morning. However, he saw his desk drawer slightly cracked open just below the radio. Ferdinand opened the drawer to discover a manila envelope inside, and within that, a pre-written resignation letter for the 20 de November Hospital. He hadn't been imagining things after all. Ferdinand put down his switchblade and shakily picked up a pen.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.15.a: There is no cost too great for security.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.16.desc:
“Thank you, gentlemen; I think you'll agree there's plenty to consider. I hope to see you soon.” After their meeting, the two AMMRI delegates were quickly ushered out of their supposed labor representative's office. They were but one interaction in one section of the grand tapestry of the PRI society. Scheduling the meeting itself was an arduous task as the delegates had to explore the Byzantine maze which was the modern-day union system. They originally were inspired by the president's willingness to accede to some of the demands made by PRI-sponsored unions.

“Do you think we did a good job? Do you think we should stick to this path?” one delegate asked another while taking a long drag on his cigarette. They were standing under a colorful awning to hide from the sun. The hot smoke did not help cool his warm body, but he needed a restorative after the long meeting.

The man they had spoken to seemed receptive, though it was uncertain what he could accomplish. After all he was merely their representative in the National Union of Social Security Workers, which is in turn part of the Federation of State Workers Unions (FSTSE), which in turn is part of the National Confederation of Popular Organizations (CNOP).

“It's not a performance; we expressed the truth in moral and legal arguments, and the rest will work itself out. Hopefully.” His partner responded with his cigarette hanging limply from his hand. As medically trained professionals, they knew that they probably shouldn't be smoking so much. They've both read the recent reports about their danger, but it hasn't stopped them. The PRI itself was like the addictive stick. Despite its danger, It had been around for so long that, at this point, it was basically impossible to achieve anything without it. “We will do whatever we can to succeed. If that means going through the state, then so be it.”
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.16.a: They will be tied into the knot of PRI labor along with the rest of the country.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.17.desc:
“In conclusion, while they pushed on some aspects of our demands, they seemed receptive to our cooperation with them.” An AMMRI delegate from the 20 de November Hospital relayed his encounter to his colleagues. Unlike sanctioned unions, their discussions with the PRI are far more unproven. The disenfranchised healthcare workers listened attentively as they sipped and stirred at early morning coffee. “It seems like our movement is working, and the more pressure we put on, the more likely we will be able to push the PRI beast into submission. I propose that in future meetings, we redouble our focus on massively increasing working and housing conditions, raises, and a total rework of the intern organization structure.”

A polite round of applause echoed in the impromptu conference room. The Mexican medical residents and interns were dedicated, well-educated, and organized; there was no way they couldn't succeed. With peace or pressure, the PRI would realize it and give them a victory the whole country would see. The assembled delegates chatted aimlessly as they waited for the next speaker to give a report. Before that could happen, a distressed man burst into the room with a large stack of newspapers.

“The paper's just come in! You guys are going to want to read this.” The pile of newspapers was split and disseminated around the association. An angry face appears with each pair of eyes that read that day's headline.

'Doctors' Union demands small raise; emphasizes PRI cooperation.'

Angry voices bounce around the room and push toward the previous speaker, who musters the courage to stand and join in the anger so that he might redirect it. “This is a complete miscarriage of the truth! The PRI and their so-called 'journals' wish to co-opt our movement for their gain. We cannot let them. They will get what they deserve and we shall take what is rightfully ours!”
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.17.a: The appearance of victory is all that matters.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.18.desc:
“...Furthermore, the salaries of doctors and resident interns shall be raised by seven percent.” The room exploded into chaos. The chairman of the AMM folded the letter and placed it back into its envelope. He would give them time to weigh their options before a decision was made.

Somewhere in the turmoil, Dr. Soliño beamed. Her family in León would never know want or hunger. She turned to Emilio, a young intern from the Federal District she had met during the previous work stoppage.

“Isn't this wonderful? I can't believe it! We won!” She pulled him into a tight hug before realizing he did not share her joy.

“This is about more than just pay now, Dr. Soliño,” Emilio retorted. “We need to keep the strike going until they recognize our union if we want to keep any of the gains we've made.” Dr. Soliño's smile faded.

“We need to be willing to negotiate, Emilio.”

“So we just roll over and take their offer? We need to guarantee fair representation in the future.”

“We won't have any representation if Ordaz thinks we'll never be satisfied!” Dr. Soliño snapped.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.18.a: The meeting is adjourned. No decision has been made.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.19.desc:
The heads of the ISSTE and the IMSS reclined on plush leather chairs in the president's office. Both men had approved of the president's plan to deploy military doctors to fill the gaps left by the strikers. They differed on the specifics. The unfortunate truth was that they did not have enough men to be everywhere at once. A single strategy would have to be chosen.

“Deploying the bulk of the doctors to the 20 de November Hospital will be the most effective strategy.” The gaunt ISSTE director explained to the president. “The Hospital is a symbol of the movement and it has served as an incubator of unrest ever since. Forcibly restoring services there during the strike will be a major blow to the dissidents.”

“On the other hand,” began the steely-haired IMSS man, “Focusing too much on one hospital means leaving the rest out to dry. Spreading the military doctors more evenly throughout the nation would bleed support for the AMM outside of the Federal District, and give us an opportunity to contain the movement in the capital.”
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.19.a: “Deploy the doctors to the 20 de November Hospital.”
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.19.b: “Send doctors to every hospital participating in the strike.”
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.20.desc:
Dr. Jareño's heart pounded as the soldiers marched on the picket line outside the 20 de November Hospital. His hands clutched the pole of the banner tighter as he came face to face with one of the uniformed goons. The soldier tore the banner from his hands before delivering a brutal left hook, sending the doctor stumbling to the ground.

After a time, he stood and massaged his head. The soldiers had already battered their way through the crowd, and had entered the building. It didn't take long for them to start dragging out the skeleton crew of doctors maintaining basic services. All the while, a growing crowd of reporters watched them like vultures circling a corpse.

Dr. Jareño did not attend the picket line the next day. He had no desire to risk his health and freedom marching brazenly in front of the army. On his way to the grocery store, he stopped to pick up today's paper from a stand. The front page of El Universal caught his eye immediately.

THE ARMY RESTORES MEDICAL SERVICES TO THE PEOPLE. Below the headline, a smiling soldier administered a syringe full of medication to a patient. The article went on and on, describing the heroic deeds of the soldiers, treating patients when doctors refused to. “Hey!” The woman running the stand knocked on the counter in front of the doctor. “Buy it or put it back.”
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.20.a: Dr. Jareño gave the woman a few pesos and disappeared down the street.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.21.desc:
In Cuernavaca, a group of doctors huddled closer together as a small column of soldiers marched towards their demonstration. The military men were well armed, and wore deep scowls under their helmets. None of the doctors were keen to force a confrontation with them. When the order to disperse was given, the medical workers exchanged glances and complied.

In Puebla, an army medic ordered a young boy to roll up his sleeve. He examines the rash on his arm, circular and scaly. The boy tries to scratch at it, and the medic slaps his hand away. “Looks like ringworm to me, it's a pain in the-” The boy's mother glared at him. “It's not easy to get rid of.”

In León, a lieutenant flipped through a filing cabinet of patient records. He was looking for the folder for one Mrs. Galván. The looping scrawl of the doctor's handwriting was proving to be quite impenetrable.

In Oaxaca, a construction worker sits in a hospital lobby, trying to keep his arm still. The limb is swollen and tender, almost certainly broken. The minutes tick by. When Julio sprained his ankle on the job during the last work stoppage, he had to wait well over an hour to be seen. It only took twenty minutes until a man in an army uniform appeared from behind a door to invite him in for treatment.
strings.MEX_Ordaz_DS.21.a: Across the nation, the hospitals return to working order.
strings.MEX_el_titan_info_tooltip:
El Titán
-------------------
It is a testament to the power of the Mexican Revolution that Ordaz now sits at its helm. Born into poverty and raised the ugly duckling of an unsupportive mother, Gustavo Díaz Ordaz has risen to preeminence with only a vast intellect and a prodigious capacity for work.

As Secretary of the Interior, those were the methods by which he wielded control over the £GFX_mex_pri_texticon PRI. Now that he bears the Presidential sash, the true strength of his £GFX_MEX_el_titan_texticon Iron grip is revealed. Vigorous discipline and firm commitment to the law are his watchwords, and the federal party and the state governors will heed his every command. His office demands no less.

In fact, his office demands more. Six years of utter devotion. Of unimaginable stress curdling his stomach. Of schemers and traitors to the Revolution lurking at home, abetted by hostile powers abroad. Of rebellious youth, £mex_dw_uns_texticon rightists, and £mex_dw_pdlp_texticon leftists looking to overthrow the order he has spent every hour of his life upholding. Six years to withstand the abyssal pressures on Mexico and on himself... or dire force will be unleashed.
strings.MEX_el_titan_tendaz_low: His Excellency sees the state like no other living man can.
strings.MEX_el_titan_tendaz_med: No man will stop His Excellency from enacting his vision.
strings.MEX_el_titan_tendaz_high: The state must survive. His Excellency will ensure it, no matter what.

strings.MEX_VEN.1.desc:
Those people comprising the business community of Caracas were very familiar with the arrivals lounge of the Maiquetía International Airport. The quality of the coffee stand, the lumpy seats and, above all, the faces of the other members that they recognized.

And so when the large party of new arrivals de-planed, off of the direct flight from Mexico City, they were immediately noticed. As was the high quality of their suits, their similar body language, and the rapidity with which local handlers from the Mexican embassy met them and directed them to waiting cars.

From those who had been close enough to the group to overhear, it was reported that the group was from Pemex, the Mexican state oil conglomerate, and were here to discuss contracts regarding oil exploitation with government officials. With great disappointment, however, none of the community were able to hear any of the group's negotiation strategies - which would have been immediately exploited.

Still, to those who heard it first, it was a small advantage, and they rushed to leverage it. Who knew what arrangement Pemex would come to with the government?
strings.MEX_VEN.2.desc:
“Our countries' friendship shall...shall...shoot”, Larrazábal sighed as he struggled to remember his words. Though the man always was one for speeches, already used to being received with thunderous and deafening applause, it didn't help that on this occasion, he would be giving a speech not in Caracas but instead to thousands of Mexicans in Veracruz's Zócalo. It was López Mateos' idea, and considering the circumstances, he felt compelled to go. Suddenly, from the corner of his eye, Larrazábal spotted his Mexican counterpart, and received a hearty greeting. “Señor Presidente,” López Mateos extended his arm, and both men shook hands. “How are you feeling?”

“Not great, if I'm being honest,” Larrazábal admitted.

“Don't worry about it, Wolfgang,” replied López Mateos. “Just hit them with the classics - death to the fascists, death to the imperialists, eternal Venezuelan-Mexican friendship yadayadayada, they'll be eating out of your hand”. López Mateos guided them up to the balcony from which they would be giving their speeches. The Mexican President instinctively grabbed the Admiral's hand and raised it into the air. The crowd roared, and the Mexican began his speech. After about ten minutes, López Mateos finished and gestured for Larrazábal to take the microphone.

For a moment, the Admiral stared blankly, as the crowd in front of him stirred in anticipation. 'Oh, what the hell, forget the speech', he thought to himself, 'just speak as you usually do.' Larrazábal then cleared his throat and spoke softly into the microphone. “My friends, my compatriots. God bless all of you, and God bless Mexico!” The crowd cheered. Larrazábal continued for a few more minutes, praising the anti-imperialist brotherhood between Venezuela and Mexico and tying themselves together economically. Just like back home, the crowd was enamored by his folksy charm, and the crowd gave Larrazábal a grandiose applause as he finished his speech. “See?” López Mateo whispered into his ear as they left the balcony “Everything went great.”
strings.MEX_VEN.3.desc:
For the small crew of the ARV Los Monjes T-13, the orders of their few officers made little sense. They were used to joking about the origins of their ship, formerly the USS LSM-548 and sold as military surplus, but were less used to the cargoes they were now loading.

To the Venezuelan sailors, the stacks of crated weaponry that had arrived from Mexico were of great interest, and they had spoken with elation at potentially getting to try them out. But that had not happened, and they had further been told, in the strongest terms, that they were to tell nobody about either the crates or their shipment of them.

They were careful to do just that - knowing that the watchful eyes of the officers were upon them - but they took every opportunity to speculate on what the weapons were to be used for. The most confusing thing was their destination - Santiago de Cuba. The Cubans could get weapons far more easily and directly than by shipping them from Mexico through Venezuela. And with the increased Caribbean activity over the past few weeks, it made even less sense. Why all this secrecy?

The sailors couldn't come to a conclusion, but they knew that whoever got the weapons would make good use of them. And as they finalized preparations and ran to carry out the lieutenant's orders, the questions seemed less important than avoiding punishment.
strings.MEX_VEN.3.a: A present - for someone at least.
strings.MEX_VEN.4.desc:
DIRECCIÓN FEDERAL DE SEGURIDAD

ISSUE: Dominican intelligence activity near Colombia's border with Venezuela accompanies military buildup.

Sources in Colombia coming from URC guerrilleros report the presence of rogue Venezuelan forces in Bucamaranga, Cúcuta, and Villa Rosaria, border cities near San Cristóbal, Venezuela. Accompanying this is a spike in activity by Dominican SIM operatives in the area, cooperating with the insurgents in their struggle against the elected government of Venezuela.

Their activity has gone unnoticed due to a breakdown of communication along the border amidst Colombia's civil war. The DFS will continue to diligently monitor the actions of the SIM to ascertain their next steps.

It is strongly recommended that the Venezuelan government is made aware of the situation if an advance response is to succeed.

Very Respectfully,
Regional Director of Security
Colonel Emilio Torres
strings.MEX_VEN.5.desc:
DIRECCIÓN FEDERAL DE SEGURIDAD

ISSUE: Dissident officers inside Venezuelan military plot rebellion with foreign backing.

The recent socialist victory in Venezuela's national elections has invigorated the subversive, right-wing sector of the Venezuelan military. According to various sources within the army, an armed insurrection is imminent. The scale, timetable, and details of such an event are still unknown.

Possible targets include the seat of power in Caracas and the various air bases and key points of entry around the country, which could put the putschists in control in a matter of hours. Some reports indicate that renegade officers in exile may also be planning an incursion through neighboring Colombia.

There is credible evidence of involvement by both Argentine and Dominican intelligence. In supporting a potential coup they seek Venezuela's political re-alignment, away from Mexico and the Veracruz Pact. The loss of Venezuela would constitute a defeat for Veracruz only comparable to losing Cuba, or Mexico itself.

It is paramount that Mexico provides the utmost support to the Venezuelan government as it confronts the subversives' next steps.

Very Respectfully,
Regional Director of Security
Colonel Emilio Torres
strings.MEX_VEN.6.desc:
The Venezuelan DIGEPOL intelligence camp outside Maracaibo reeked of sweat, ink, and an anxious desperation. Venezuelan officers leaned over maps with their Mexican SNI counterparts, their eyes tracing over a faint line from Colombia's border straight into San Cristóbal.

“Villa de Rosario... Cúcuta... Bucaramanga...” the SNI agent muttered under his breath, underlining each name on the map with a worn-out pen. “All roads point straight to Maracaibo. This is how they're getting their information.”

The Venezuelan officers soured, exchanging grim looks with each other. They had already suspected San Cristóbal to be the first domino in a coming coup by dissident officers. And Maracaibo seemed to be the second domino.

A folder slid across the table, grainy photos fanning across to show shady couriers hopping the Colombian border on their way to Maracaibo. No doubt they were the ones coordinating and masterminding the coup's follow-up after San Cristóbal.

The Mexican agent took out his knife, slamming it downwards onto the map. “This is one of their main arteries. Blockade Maracaibo. Shore up the border patrols. Maybe shoot some of those pests running around the countryside.” He looked back at the Venezuelan officers. “And after that, my friends, there'll be nothing left of the coup, nothing after San Cristóbal.”

The camp fell silent. Although they didn't know it yet, the decision at the Maracaibo camp would not only ripple across Venezuela but also light the fires of a new friendship between two nations.
strings.MEX_VEN.7.desc:
The blue-grey smoke from Fidel Castro's Cohiba floated under the ceiling of the office in Miraflores like a storm cloud. The Cuban leader stood by the window, gazing at the lights of Caracas, but his eyes reflected another city-the one boiling with rapture in January of '59.

“Do you remember Plaza O'Leary, Fabricio?” Castro's voice sounded unusually quiet, almost intimate. “Do you remember that sea of people? You introduced me to the crowd as a brother back then. And when I, foolishly, mentioned Betancourt's name, they booed him so hard my ears popped.” Fidel turned, steel flashing in his gaze. “Your people knew who their enemy was even back then. They waited for a revolution, but got a compromise. Do not repeat this mistake.”

Ojeda wearily rubbed his temples. The memory burned him: back then he was a hero who toppled a dictator, and now he felt like a cornered beast. “Now they aren't whistling at politicians, Fidel. Now they are cleaning weapons in the barracks to take my head off.”

Adolfo López Mateos, sitting in the shadows with the impassivity of a sphinx, coughed delicately. “Historical parallels are beautiful gentlemen, but we need a strategy. DIGEPOL and the SNI are working to exhaustion, we are exposing conspirator cells, but time is working against us.”

“To hell with time,” Castro cut in, chopping the air with his hand. “In '59, I said in that square: 'Venezuela is the homeland of the Liberator, and she must lead America.' Do not let some parquet generals take that right away from you, brother. My 'tourists' are already on planes. If the army rolls out tanks, they will meet veterans of the Sierra Maestra. We will turn this palace into a fortress against which they will break their teeth.”
strings.MEX_VEN.8.desc:
Silence hung in the office, heavy as the pre-storm sky over Mount Ávila. Fidel Castro nervously paced the room, and every glance he cast toward Raúl Leoni was steeped in coldness. The Venezuelan President, whose massive, husky frame towered over the desk, maintained a monumental calm. He did not interrupt, but merely listened intently, clasping his large hands together as the Cuban vented his energy.

“Fate loves cruel jokes, Raúl,” Castro said, stopping by the map. “Your rangers hunt my students in the jungles, yet today I offer you the only thing that can hold up your throne - Cuban bayonets. Say the word, and we will turn Miraflores into an impregnable fortress that the generals will break their teeth on.”

Leoni slowly shook his head. There was no fear in his voice, only the reasonableness of a man accustomed to finding the safe path. “I appreciate the gesture, Fidel. But Venezuela is a complicated family. If a single one of your soldiers steps onto the cobblestones of Caracas, the army will rise against a 'Red intervention.' I cannot risk civil peace for the sake of my own security.”

Adolfo López Mateos, sensing the moment, intervened gently. “Then let the guns speak, but from the sea. The Mexican squadron will anchor in the roadstead of La Guaira. Destroyers in the distance will restrain those barracks hotheads better than foreign infantry in Libertador.”

Leoni paused, weighing the risks, and finally nodded. Mexican steel on the horizon was the most sensible and measured choice.
strings.MEX_VEN.9.desc:
The atmosphere in the cabinet was taut as a guitar string before it snapped. Fidel Castro shifted in his chair, trying not to meet the Venezuelan President's eyes. The Comandante, accustomed to the company of rough “barbudos” and the smell of gunpowder, felt out of his element next to Gonzalo Barrios - a man of impeccable manners, subtle perfume, and soft gestures. To Castro, this “intellectual” was the embodiment of everything the revolution should sweep away, but politics dictated its own strange alliances.

“The situation is shit, Gonzalo,” the Cuban grunted, studying the toe of his boot. “Your generals smell weakness. They see before them not a leader and they need the language of strength. My boys can provide that language. A special forces regiment in Miraflores - and any colonel will think ten times before ordering an assault.”

Barrios carefully adjusted his shirt cuffs. He read the squeamishness in his guest's posture perfectly, but his voice remained even and calm. “I appreciate your candor, Fidel. But the legitimacy of my government rests on the crystal foundation of the constitution, not on foreign bayonets. If the people see Cubans on the palace balconies, they will decide I have sold the country to the communists. That would be a gift to the rebels that I do not intend to give.”

Adolfo López Mateos, for whom personal antipathies mattered little in the face of geopolitics, intervened with his usual businesslike manner. “Then we will demonstrate strength without touching the ground. The Mexican squadron will enter territorial waters. Blockade the ports, control the coast. This will show the army that the world is on our side, but will not give them grounds to scream about occupation.”

Barrios nodded, a flicker of relief in his eyes. The grey hulls of Mexican destroyers - that was an elegant argument, quite in his style.
strings.MEX_VEN.10.desc:
I hope you have been doing a lot of good in Cuba. I always hear the most excellent things about the state of affairs under your rule.

As you know, fate has not been as kind to us here in Venezuela. I write to you today to kindly request your aid in maintaining the legitimacy of our government in the unlikely case that the reactionaries, with their devious machinations, manage to destroy our hard-won gains. Should they succeed, Fidel, I am sure that you will jump to an old friend's aid and help me get out of Venezuela, where my life would be threatened. From the safety of your country, we will continue our struggle for the just rule of our people.

Although I did not start this letter with the most optimism, I truly believe we will be able to push the putschist swine back and do away with their stink once and for all, especially if you provide us with your support. When the dust is settled, Venezuela and Cuba will stand side by side against imperialism, colonialism and usher in a new age for the common people of Latin America. I await the day with glee...
strings.MEX_VEN.11.desc:
President López Mateos.

Time is short and of the essence, and so I ask you to forgive me if I do not fill this missive with all the platitudes you deserve.

I'm sure you have already been notified of the plot by reactionary elements in our army to depose our democracy. I ask you, therefore, for two things.

First, my government will, of course, require all support you can afford to give us in the upcoming trial, particularly should the putschists succeed in their endeavour and exile us. Of course, all of this is moot if we end up in their hands, and so I personally humbly request that you allow me and the rest of my men refuge in the Mexican embassy, followed by swift transport to Mexico, from where we can continue our operations until the illegitimate government collapses.

Trust me when I say that I do not ask for your help without due cause; rather, I find there is no other choice as the worst scenario we could have conceived unfurled, threatening the security of both of our nations and Latin America as a whole.

Warm regards,
strings.MEX_VEN.12.desc:
His Excellency, López Mateos.

As you have surely been informed already, shortly there will begin a struggle for the soul of Venezuela. It is not simply our revolution that is threatened here, but the very fabric of our Latin American societies. Mexico must be involved in this clash of ideologies. Should the reactionaries win, not only shall it severely weaken the Veracruz Pact by overthrowing one of its founding members, but it will also set the stage for further counterrevolutionary activities across national borders, allowing the shackles of imperialism and colonialism to reappear and imprison us all.

Every Venezuelan who has yet to fall to the honeyed words of the enemy is currently toiling to prevent the worst from passing. But the non-negligible possibility of the coup's success cannot be ignored, and so we must prepare for it just as well. For that dreaded future, I humbly request your oath that we will receive asylum in the embassy, then swift transport to Mexico, where we will be able to continue our fight against the illegitimate and tyrannical government that will undoubtedly spring up in our stead.

As we continue the battle on the ground, we await your response with worry and bated breath.
strings.MEX_VEN.13.desc:
Luis Ignacio Rodríguez Taboada did not expect evacuation planning to be part of his ambassadorial duties. And yet, here he was, talking with the President of Venezuela on the topic. “Certainly, certainly, but just in case you need it, do know it is an option... Oh, I understand, I am certain that we will be victorious as well, but it remains... yes, no worries, I will have someone wait for you.” Luis hung up and sighed his stress away. Around him, staffers were working around the clock to prepare everything for potential evacuation. Taboada smiled at their dedication to preserving Venezuela's own revolution. A seed for internationalism, perhaps.

The Mexican ambassador checked that all the curtains were drawn, a safety measure only. Receding gunshots could still be heard at regular intervals in the city and, if one listened carefully, the shouts of men engaged in battle were also audible. Still, the President's tone seemed certain that the putschists would be beaten back.

As he approached the last room he had yet to check the windows of, he heard the faint mutterings of someone inside. As soon as he opened the door, he saw one of his staff members kneeling down in prayer: “Hail Mary Most Holy, Beloved Daughter of God the Father...”

Taboada stood there observing for a few seconds, somewhat shocked by the display.

“Grant your good success to this request...”Then, with a headshake, he continued his round, internally scoffing at the backwardness of it all. But if these superstitions made these hard-working people feel better and did not interfere, he was willing to accept them.
strings.MEX_VEN.13.a: Defend this good country from those who seek its destruction.“
strings.MEX_VEN.14.desc:
Taboada lowered the telegram onto the lacquered surface of his desk. In the silence of the Mexican ambassador's office, broken only by the hum of the air conditioner, the old diplomat felt a lump rise in his throat. Not from fear, but from a fierce, triumphant satisfaction.

Before his eyes flashed the gray, despair-soaked Marseille of the forties. He remembered that sticky terror: endless columns of refugees clogging the roads of France, fleeing the Nazi darkness. He remembered the eyes of Spanish Republicans begging for a visa before the Vichy police handed them over to Franco's executioners or sent them in cattle cars to the East, to the ovens of the death camps. Back then, roads were arteries through which the blood of a dying Europe flowed.

But the report from San Cristóbal told a different story. The Venezuelans used their trucks and buses not for flight, but as weapons. They turned the streets into steel clots, stopping the infection of fascism. Castro León, that pocket-sized Führer in epaulets, counted on a fast win, but he hit a wall against which far more formidable armies had shattered - the fury of people with nothing left to lose.

Taboada wiped his hand across his face, erasing the haunting past. In Europe, he had watched nations break under the tracks of a “Tiger.” Here, force broke against the crossed arms of workers. He reached for the phone to relay the news to Mexico City. This time, unlike in the cursed year of 1942, he would not have to issue visas for the doomed.
strings.MEX_VEN.14.a: This time, the Republic fought back.
strings.MEX_VEN.15.desc:
Taboada allowed himself a rare luxury - undoing the top button of his shirt and pouring two fingers of mezcal, which he had been saving for a special occasion. The burning liquid reminded him of the taste of dust on the roads of Guanajuato, the taste of those distant years when they smoked the fanatic “Cristeros” out of mountain ravines. General Castro León, that hapless little Napoleon, painfully reminded the ambassador of the old Mexican caciques: just as much arrogance, just as much gold on the uniform, and the same fatal misunderstanding that the time of the haciendas was gone forever.

The Iberian puppeteers thought they could smuggle the counter-revolution through the back door, using secret paths from Cúcuta like contraband tobacco. They counted on a blitzkrieg, on fear, on apathy. But they forgot an old revolutionary truth that Taboada had learned as a lieutenant: if you go against the people, make sure you have enough bullets to shoot every last one of them. León did not. His “Grand Army” crumbled, colliding with the icy contempt of the streets and the locked gates of the factories.

The ambassador smirked, looking out at the lights of evening Caracas. History loves to rhyme: reaction had once again choked on its own bile, just as it had half a century ago in his homeland. He finished the mezcal, adjusted his tie, and called for a car. It was time. The President was waiting for him at Miraflores - and this time, not to trace evacuation routes with trembling hands, but to smoke the cigar of victors.
strings.MEX_VEN.15.a: Worthy heirs of Bolívar. Send our congratulations to Caracas!
strings.MEX_VEN.15.a.tt: With the triumph of the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan people over reactionary coupists and their {ibr_getflag} backers, our {mex_getflag} Veracruz ally will now be a vital partner for many years to come.
strings.MEX_VEN.16.desc:
When Luis Ignacio Rodríguez Taboada left Mexico and its hectic politics to serve as ambassador to Venezuela, he never thought he would have to plan for their exfiltration from their own country. And yet, this was the task laid out for him now.

“Yes, of course. I will have someone at the embassy's gates to look for you. Please be safe.” Luis slammed the telephone down and rested his head on the table for just a moment. Then, he fixed his posture and looked around at the staff, paralyzed by the frequent shouts and gunshots that resounded in the city. “Come on, comrades! Don't stand there doing nothing. I understand you are scared, but we cannot let our Venezuelan comrades down.” He sighed as the staff only reluctantly obeyed, and massaged his temples to soothe the pain of his migraine, muttering profanities under his breath.

Taboada checked items off his mental list. The curtains were drawn, the families of senior officials taken care of, and Mexico City had been contacted for evacuation. He exited the building onto the embassy's premises to ensure the rounds he had set were being completed, only to find the three staffers he had assigned kneeling, their hands joined in prayer: “We seek refuge under your protection, O Holy Mother of God...”

“What the hell are you...” Taboada's hands turned into clenched fists. He took a deep breath in, deciding that yelling and anger would not solve anything. “My friends, your superstitions could cost the President of our brotherly Venezuela his life, you can't let it cloud your judgment. We must act, not pray.”

The staffers did not even look at him as they continued reciting.
strings.MEX_VEN.17.desc:
From the balcony of the Miraflores Palace, Fabricio Ojeda felt the city shiver. Caracas at night was always glimmering, not only by the city lights, but also by hope. However, some glimmers didn't shine like the rest. In the quiet night, Fabricio Ojeda could barely hear shells. In the distance, he could see tanks moving below the hill. The ground underneath him trembled faintly, but its shockwaves didn't remind him of a military parade, more so invasion.

“President Ojeda,” a hurried voice called from behind him. A uniformed officer, gasping for breath. “San Cristóbal, Mérida, and Maracaibo have fallen. Enemy insurgents have already entered Caracas. You need to go. Now!”

The next moments felt like hours, dissolving into fragments. The hurried footsteps, his wife clutching his arm, the rotors tearing through the night.

As he looked below the helicopter, he saw Caracas up in fiery infernos, neighborhoods filled with nothing but smoke and screams of horror. There was no story to be told here, no lesson to be learned, for words could not tell the sheer scale of hopelessness he could feel.

The helicopter jolted as it landed at the Mexican embassy, a fortress even Castro León wouldn't dare fire at. Floodlights scanned the perimeter. Soldiers scrambled around, with no one sure if the insurgents were crazy enough to invoke Mexico's wrath. But Luis Ignacio Rodríguez Taboada, the Mexican ambassador, was waiting patiently for Ojeda. His weary face had already foretold the dire news.

“Caracas has fallen.”
strings.MEX_VEN.18.desc:
In the dead of night, the Miraflores Palace still whispered with activity, though it would be the last time Gonzalo Barrios and Raúl Leoni would see their lavish chandeliers, would dig their feet into the velvet cushions, would admire the exquisite portraits of the great leaders that preceded them. It was the last oasis of friendship in a country with a dying light.

“You ever think,” Leoni mused, staring at the bottom of his wine glass, “we might live long enough to see Venezuela stop tearing itself apart?”

Barrios gave a dry chuckle. “I think she's already found her peace.”

Just then, the door burst open. A young officer, pale with urgency, quickly saluted before blurting out his report. “Señor Presidente, Eastern Caracas has fallen. You both need to be evacuated immediately.

Barrios jolted from his chair. ”What is going on out there?“

Leoni slowly rose. ”Seems like we can never be too complacent in a country like this.“ He exhaled with disappointment. ”Go. I'll gather my family.“

Barrios hesitated, but the officer was already pushing him out. Within minutes, they were airlifted to Venezuela's last asylum left: the Mexican embassy. The trip blurred, clouded by more despondency than actual fear. Venezuela was always a ticking time bomb; Barrios just expected a little more time.

Luis Ignacio Rodríguez Taboada waited at the embassy gates. The Mexican ambassador's words would deliver the final death blow to the Gaitanismo that thought they could revitalize Venezuela:

”Caracas has fallen.“
strings.MEX_VEN.19.desc:
The clock in Leoni's office ticked louder that night, each second reminding the Venezuelan leader that his time had already run out. The door burst open; a pale officer stood at attention. “Sir - Eastern Caracas has broken into infighting. We must evacuate you to the Mexican embassy, now!”

Leoni jolted to his feet, pushing his chair back. “What's going on?” Before he could even get an answer, he was pulled out of his office, leaving the pens behind that had forged Venezuela into a republic.

Outside, his wife, Menca, called for a headcount of their children: “One. Two. Three. Four.” But her voice stopped and her face turned pale. Álvaro, their youngest, was missing.

Panic swept through the group. Thoughts ran through Leoni's mind. What if his son were lost? Injured? Dead? All Leoni could think about was saving his son, being there for someone who needed his guidance. He must be able to save his son, for he couldn't save his country.

The boy's wails revealed his position, and in no time, a guard quickly scooped him up before delivering him to his mother's arms. One last salute was exchanged between Leoni and the guards before the family flew off into the night sky to the one last asylum in Caracas.

Caracas burned below. But the whizzing of shells and thundering of tanks made the guess as to who was winning trivial. Waiting at the embassy, Luis Ignacio Rodríguez Taboada greeted the family as they landed. Leoni helped each one of his children down from the helicopter, his wife still trying to calm down the crying Álvaro. But Álvaro was young enough not to understand the weight of the words that would come out of the ambassador's mouth:

“Caracas has fallen.”
strings.MEX_VEN.20.desc:
REPORT ON VENEZUELAN COUP
DIRECCIÓN DE SEGURIDAD INTERNACIONAL
ISSUE: Coup in Venezuela Topples Government

At 4:20 AM, Jesús María Castro León and dissident Venezuelan officers crossed the Colombian border into San Cristóbal, forcing the local garrison to retreat. Within hours, Vega de Aza and El Vigía fell to the putschists, allowing them to control both the roadways and the skies. Maracaibo and Barquisimeto subsequently fell.

Twelve hours since the coup began, Caracas was abandoned to the insurgents. The president and his family have been exiled under Mexican protection.

Following the evacuation, Castro León had been sworn in as President, ending democratic rule in the country.

The importance of Venezuela cannot be underestimated. A pillar of the Veracruz Pact has been broken. Besides Cuba, Mexico now stands alone in the proxy battleground that is Central America. Venezuela has been torn from our grasp, and we fear there is nothing we can do now that the coup has finished. History will remember us bitterly for allowing this transgression.

We should have done more, Su Excelencia.

With great remorse,
Colonel Rangel Escamilla
strings.MEX_VEN.20.a: Apologies cannot forgive us for our hesitation.
strings.MEX_VEN.20.a.tt: With the fall of our {ven_getflag} Venezuelan ally to military rule, our {mex_getflag} Veracruz dream has been dealt a dire, perhaps fatal wound.
strings.MEX_VEN.24.desc:
“Su Excelencia, a call from the embassy in Caracas.”

A curt nod, with a barely suppressed grimace. Ordaz brought the handset to his ear, and before the ambassador could speak he began, “He's done it hasn't he?”

“Si. He will announce it today, sir, from Miraflores,” the ambassador said. They had discussed the rumblings in Caracas in their last call, about Venezuelan President Ojeda's decision to nationalize his country's oil industry. A terrible headache, to think what the Americans would say about that.

Ordaz was already scrambling to the closest television, tuning to Telesistema Mexicano. Yellow, blue and red flooded the screen. Ojeda spoke to a teeming crowd from a balcony, denouncing the “long darkness of subjugation to the dollar.”

Ordaz rubbed his temples raw as Ojeda announced the introduction of a bill to nationalize the oil industry for the people of Venezuela. The people erupted into wild cheering, pushing Mexico's reporters along a tide of drums and chants towards the National Assembly palace.

“Send the Venezuelans a message,” Ordaz rattled off, “tell them this is a sensitive issue.”

“But, Mr. Ojeda...”

“Secure a meeting with him as soon as possible. Try to talk him out of this, please.”

The call that followed was with another ambassador: America's, in Mexico City. Ordaz chewed the sides of his mouth as he calmly assured the furious American that, no, Venezuela would surely be stopped by her Mexican older brother. The U.S would not have their industries stolen from them.

The complaints still ringing in his ear, Ordaz hunched over his desk. He needed to figure out his next steps, quickly.
strings.MEX_VEN.24.a: Lean hard - get Ojeda to tone this nonsense down and moderate his message.
strings.MEX_VEN.24.b: The gringos trust us... but there's not much we can do.
strings.MEX_VEN.24.tt:
If {ven_getflag} Ojeda's government remains stronger than the military and democratic opposition, {mex_getflag} our interests in Venezuela will prevail over {ibr_getflag} Iberia and the {usa_getflag} U.S.
------------------------------------
strings.MEX_VEN.25.desc:
A secretary peeked her head into Salinas's office. “Su Excelencia, a call from the embassy in Caracas.”

Salinas waved her away, and shushed the governor of Zacatecas, who'd come for some nonsense meeting. Handset to his ear, he said, “Good morning. Ojeda's announcement?”

“It's happening today, sir,” he said, breathless. They had discussed the rumblings in Caracas in their last call, about Venezuelan President Ojeda's decision to nationalize his country's oil industry, but there was no timetable then. Salinas had been anticipating this call.

“He is announcing it from Miraflores,” the ambassador added, and Salina motioned for the governor to find the remote and tune to Telesistema Mexicano. Yellow, blue and red flooded the screen. Ojeda spoke to a teeming crowd from a balcony, denouncing the “long darkness of subjugation to the dollar.”

Salinas was tight-lipped, watching Ojeda reveal a bill to nationalize the oil industry for the people of Venezuela. The people erupted into wild cheering, pushing Mexico's reporters along a tide of drums and chants towards the National Assembly palace.

“Su Excelencia, our response?”

Thank you for notifying me quickly,“ Salinas said, slowly. ”As for our response... I want a message delivered to President Ojeda. Keep it brief. Polite.“

”Is there anything you'd like the President to hear, sir?“

Salinas breathed sharply. ”I don't want my thoughts to be revealed if this gets leaked to the press.“
strings.MEX_VEN.25.a: “Let him know, at least, that this is a step in the right direction.”
strings.MEX_VEN.25.b: “Tell him I send my regards, but be non-committal.”
strings.MEX_VEN.26.desc:
A secretary peeked her head into Madrazo's office. “Su Excelencia, a call from the embassy in Caracas.”

A curt nod. Madrazo adjusted his tie out of habit, as if for a face-to-face meeting. Handset to his ear, and before the ambassador could speak, he began, “Ojeda's announcement?”

“It's happening today, sir,” he said, breathless. They had discussed the rumblings in Caracas in their last call, about Venezuelan President Ojeda's decision to nationalize his country's oil industry, but there was no timetable then. Had that changed?

“He is announcing it from Miraflores,” the ambassador added, and Madrazo was already scrambling to the closest television, tuning to Telesistema Mexicano. Yellow, blue and red flooded the screen. Ojeda spoke to a teeming crowd from a balcony, denouncing the “long darkness of subjugation to the dollar.”

Madrazo laughed dryly, as Ojeda announced the introduction of a bill to nationalize the oil industry for the people of Venezuela. The people erupted into wild cheering, pushing Mexico's reporters along a tide of drums and chants towards the National Assembly palace.

“Thank you for the information,” Madrazo rattled off, and immediately called Miraflores. Ojeda picked up quickly enough, his voice on the other side still winded from the speech.

“I take it you know,” he said, and there was also excitement coursing through those historic words. Madrazo grinned to himself.

“Yes, Mr. President, and I congratulate you. No one else has dared take such a bold step against our northern neighbor's imperialism before. These next few months will surely be difficult. Mexico and Veracruz are with you,” he said, then paused, frowning...
strings.MEX_VEN.26.a: And we'll give you full support. Everything we have.
strings.MEX_VEN.26.b: As long as it is reasonable.
strings.MEX_VEN.27.desc:
DIRECCIÓN FEDERAL DE SEGURIDAD

ISSUE: Suspect officers building ties with Venezuelan opposition.

Surveillance indicates developing relationships between military circles and civilian opponents to Venezuelan president Fabricio Ojeda. Led by members of Acción Democratica and the right-wing section of the URD, concerns about President Ojeda's decision to nationalize the oil industry has spurred them to action.

The military and civilian opposition share anxieties of Ojeda as a “second Fidel.” Together, it's clear they intend to compel his abdication by force, if necessary.

It's urgently advised that Mexico take all necessary measures to bolster the legitimacy of Ojeda's government. Otherwise, it may face a fatal crisis.

Very Respectfully, 
Regional Director of Security
Colonel Emilio Torres.
strings.MEX_VEN.27.a: We'll flag suspect officers and notify our Venezuelan partners.
strings.MEX_VEN.27.b: Surveil the opposition's activities, find the skeletons in their closet.
strings.MEX_VEN.27.c: Hold a photo-op at the Veracruz Forum, celebrate Venezuela's Ojedista leaders.
strings.MEX_VEN.28.desc:
It started with DIGEPOL's warning as part of the daily briefings. “Suspicious exchanges” between his most bitter enemies in Acción Democratica and the military. He read every line in a crawl, tongue going numb. “Surveillance indicates growing radicalization of the opposition.”

A hard knock. Ojeda staggered, going upright behind the vastness of his desk. As if it would protect him from...

It was only an aide, cracking the door open. No gun barrel glint. “Mr. President, five minutes to leave for the conference.”

“Cancel.” A dead silence. Ojeda snatched his documents, the DIGEPOL report, with sweaty hands. “Cancel the conference, Gladys. I'm not going.”

That night, he made international calls. Fidel Castro's voice echoed in his office, and Ojeda let out a bitter chuckle, knowing such a conversation was the exact sort of thing his enemies would call him a traitor for.

“Something's shifting, Fidel. It isn't a petty squabble anymore, with the Adecos and Urredistas.”

“What do you mean, Fabricio?”

“I don't know how many dissident officers remain after Holy Wednesday, but they do. Only a matter of time before a coup.” Ojeda rubbed the bags in his eyes. “I already asked the Mexicans. If you sent intelligence personnel here it would be a game changer...”

“That would be very risky, Cuban soldiers in Venezuela.” Fidel sighed on the other side of the line. “But your opposition already thinks we're too close. The Veracruz Pact binds us, so I could send a few militiamen to Caracas, for your sake.”
strings.MEX_VEN.28.a: “Intelligence only. That will reduce the risk and stop this threat.”
strings.MEX_VEN.28.b: “Damn the risk, without Cuban security assets, I and the revolution are as good as dead.”
strings.MEX_VEN.29.desc:
Chaos. Ojeda had long accepted that the nationalization bill wouldn't go through that day, much to his chagrin. The floor of the assembly had been uncontrollable from the moment the nationalisation bill had been introduced, and nothing could help it. He had used the time to negotiate with a few moderates - some progress had been made, but even with some opponents gone, he could feel hesitation beginning to creep in. Turning his head, Ojeda shouted swears at Rafael Caldera, for morale if nothing else.

And then, it stopped ahead of schedule. A police officer first advanced a statement to a speaker long rendered useless, then chose to proclaim, foghorn and all, that a car had crashed into the barricade. Suddenly rendered mute, the assembly chose to heed his warning and chose to disperse. Enraged, Ojeda excused himself to the bathroom, only leaving after them with dejection visible on a face he hadn't dried.

As he stormed home, everything was quiet. No guitars strummed from the walls, and the radios didn't even blare with static. The bars were totally empty, with no queues streaming out like usual. No street vendors struggled to sell their wares, nor did cars pass him by. If it wasn't for distant creaks, Ojeda would have been totally alone. But his thoughts, by now, were racing, as were his legs. Back to Cuba. Back to Batista, and the night before his ousting. The calm before the storm.

Slamming the door shut, he quickly turned to his bags. He threw a few items in - clothes that had just been washed, identification he didn't need - before stopping. Through the mail, he could see familiar insignia. Both Fidel Castro and {mex_getleader} had written. With how important the nationalization bill was, he didn't need to be told the significance of their contents. Choosing to take himself to bed, his fingers nonetheless floated over the Mexican envelope, and his eyes flicked over a random line.
strings.MEX_VEN.29.a: “...it will take unity between you and the Venezuelan people to withstand the reactionary...”
strings.MEX_VEN.29.b: “...maintain your resolve in these times, and stick to your liberatory agenda...”
strings.MEX_VEN.29.c: “...situation is too dangerous right now, but our embassy remains open should you wish...”
strings.MEX_VEN.30.desc:
The scenes on screen almost played out like a movie. As the first cracks of dawn began to rise across the skyline, tanks and trucks rolled down streets surrounding the National Assembly. Behind them roared a mass of cars, filled with demonstrators and congressional opponents to the nationalization bill. They knew what was coming next; they'd block any Ojedistas from the chamber, advance a no-confidence motion, and then leave the nationalization bill to die. All it would take was time.

A mess of cars met them. This coup had been expected, and these loyalists had been preparing to counteract them. From a mass of cars and counterdemonstrators, and guided by agents with Mexican and Cuban accents, a barricade was quickly brought up, backed by protesters on both sides. Soon, any progress was halted, and a small corridor opened only so that socialists could come through; a confidence measure by itself.

Then, just as the wave crested, it buckled. Rumored arrests soon became replaced with real ones, lists of coup-plotters being dragged out of the crowd in handcuffs by loyalists within the Venezuelan military. A military presence remained, watching over the bands of Ojedistas with mild disgust, but did little more than shake their heads at chants. As the sky tipped from navy to light blue, the military began to disperse, their withdrawal immediately celebrated by those who hadn't yet escaped.

Within the rooms of the Presidential Palace, work had basically stopped. The first parts of this live broadcast were now reaching virtually every room, flat reports from the Telesistema Mexicano being watched, and cheered on, by a growing number of staff members, eschewing their work for a brief moment to celebrate the survival of Ojeda's government. For a brief moment, {mex_getleader} appeared behind them, hovering only to watch the news confirm that nationalization was still going ahead.
strings.MEX_VEN.31.desc:
For the briefest of moments, Fabricio Ojeda sat down in relief. There were still ways he could lose, and for the coup to resurge, but it looked less likely by the minute. With how embedded the opposition had been, too, they would likely not be able to make up the numbers, as he had feared the night before. As long as this peace held, it could just go through. Just then, a phone rung, and by impulse, Ojeda lunged for it.

“So, I hear that you survived another coup, Fabricio?” asked a familiar voice.

“Ah, Fidel, glad that the news have escaped Caracas!” he replied, smiling. “Have to say, it could've easily gone the other way last night.”

“I could imagine, with how many forces tried to oust you. The Noticiero Nacional is filled with scenes of celebration within Caracas, but looking out of my window, it almost feels like I'm right there with you.”

“I'm very happy to hear that. With this nationalization bill coming up, I know we're going to do wonderful things for Latin America.” His eyes drew up to the clock. The vote was almost about to happen. “Look, I'd love to talk further, but the vote's coming up, and it'd be grim if I missed it.” A brief farewell came from the other side, cut off as he hung up.

Rising from his chair, Ojeda paced into his car, looking at the streets. Cars were strewn about, but most people still remaining simply walked past, idly looking ahead. Entering into the chamber to a chorus of applause, he looked around. No sign of many assemblymen; it seemed that they had largely taken leave, either to prison or the streets. With nary a complaint, the nationalization bill passed through. Tighter than he hoped, and a few moderates seemed to have moved against it, but there were far too many abstentions to jeopardize its majority.
strings.MEX_VEN.32.desc:
For a brief moment, the Cuban embassy in Caracas was completely silent, enraptured by the news above. Luis Augusto Dubuc, stressed and unkempt, hesitated as he gave his presidential speech, promising fire, fury, and peace at once. Below, and well outside of the halls of the Senado, Ojeda gathered with his wife and remaining loyalists, straining to remember every phone line still open. As the room continued to speak, attempted calls to the Mexican embassy gave nothing but a ringtone, a muted wa-

“Fabricio, is that you?” asked a familiar voice from down the line. Ojeda gave a sigh of relief as he raised a thumb.

“Fidel, it's good to hear from you.” Ojeda turned around to look at his cabinet, now huddling closer to his edge of the table.

Silence came down the line, but only for a moment. “Your misfortunes won't end here. The Venezuelan army is under Congress's control, arresting anybody who looks red. You'll be prosecuted the moment you step out of that embassy.”

The news came as no surprise, but Ojeda still swore under his breath. “Well, we can't stay here, surely? Mexico's embassy is larger, but they've not reached out to us since the nationalization bill failed.”

Another silence came, this time longer, and now even more unnerving. “I can't answer for Mexico. Havana will welcome you with open arms, but you'll have to get there first. Our agents might be able to help, but you'll have to act fast, and that's as far as my influence will go.”

“Thank you, I'll bear that in mind,” replied Ojeda, his smile collapsing into a grimace. How could he escape? Every second wasted was one in which another agent was found, another street swarmed, another lifeline cut. And yet, where could he start?
strings.MEX_VEN.32.a: All the while, the lifelines northwards remained totally mute.
strings.MEX_VEN.33.desc:
Across the office, the flames burnt softly, their flickers drowned out by frantic calls between Cuban agents, and by the desperate cataloguing of rumors and military interviews blaring from the television overhead. Papers detailing minutes of calls between Ojeda and Cuba burned amidst files on military positions and profiles on individual generals whose loyalties had now been made very clear. A knock came on the door, forcing the guns of every agent upwards, readied as one inched towards opening it.

“Damn it, Yolanda, are you trying to alert everybody in Caracas?” asked the agent, only lowering his gun slightly as he noticed the crowd behind her. “And who the hell are these people?”

Yolanda forced herself in, momentarily remaining quiet as they streamed in. “Mexican agents, and socialist deputies from the Democratic Republican Union, Emilio,” she growled, looking over the remaining piles. “Have you heard the news? The military has called a state of emergency, and is going through each building for more Ojedists to arrest.”

The other Cuban agents sullied themselves, before one deputy, wiping his forehead of sweat, raised a hand. “I wasn't able to call Ojeda before being swept up in this. Do you have any clue where he is?”

The agent to the back shook his head. “No clue. He and the Minister of Internal Affairs have just disappeared. Most of their cabinet didn't attend the vote, and those who did are being taken by us to Aruba now. Best to presume that they're dead.”

By now, a few sirens could be distantly heard. Finally, Yolanda sighed, halting one agent. “Most of this office is clear, and I don't think we have enough time for the rest,” she peered outside, and then to the new group, “and our planned escape should still have enough room for these people. Best to leave, at least for now.”
strings.MEX_VEN.33.a: And so, the withdrawal heads north.
strings.MEX_VEN.34.desc:
Diplomatic Cable from Luis I. Rodríguez, Ambassador to Venezuela
Top Secret - Exclusively for Secretary Manuel Tello Baurraud

Mexican - Venezuelan relations proceeding smoothly following the inauguration of Unión Republicana Democrática politician Jóvito Villalba as President. A liberal, Villalba made remarks during the campaign that could be construed as critical of our revolutionary governing system, primarily as attacks on his leftist Acción Democrática opponent. Since assuming office, however, Villalba has maintained cordial and extensive contact with our embassy, taking on the role of a pragmatic and cooperative statesman.
