His government is almost exclusively focused on further reforms to institutionalize Venezuela's democracy. Should President Villalba succeed, our Venezuelan ally will be further strengthened and stabilized. The dominant performance of the URD, AD, and the Christian social democrat COPEI parties in the past elections has shown that reactionaries are incapable of competing at the ballot box in Venezuela. Our contacts in Caracas suggest that the rightists may be forming dissident groups in response.

Having discussed the matter with President Villalba, he has requested that Venezuela's intelligence service, DIGEPOL, be formally admitted into the Oficina Conjunta de Asuntos Externos. He believes that OCAE, the intelligence coordination body established between our DFS and the Cuban DGI, should be sufficient to identify and address any threats to the Venezuelan government and revolution.
strings.MEX_VEN.34.a: I consider this a significant victory for the Veracruz alliance.
strings.MEX_VEN.35.desc:
Diplomatic Cable from Luis I. Rodríguez, Ambassador to Venezuela
Top Secret - Exclusively for Secretary Manuel Tello Baurraud

Mexican - Venezuelan relations proceeding following the inauguration of COPEI politician Rafael Caldera as President. A self-described 'Christian Social Democrat', Caldera was perhaps the least desirable candidate in contention, representing the reintroduction of clerical influence into Venezuelan politics. In personal matters, however, I have found Caldera to be both amiable and reasonable, with multiple high-profile visits to our embassy to discuss proceedings at the Veracruz Forum. Additionally, he has made anti-fascism a key part of his domestic platform and recent speech to the OAS. Diplomatically at least, Caldera could be a significant asset.

President Caldera's victory, while unfortunate, reassured many religious conservatives about the course of the Venezuelan revolution, further stabilizing the country. With COPEI dominant at the ballot box, our contacts in Caracas suggest that the small contingent of irreconcilable rightists will drop out of the electoral system entirely and may organize into armed dissident groups.

After discussing the matter with President Caldera, he has requested that Venezuela's intelligence service, DIGEPOL, be formally admitted into the Oficina Conjunta de Asuntos Externos. He believes that OCAE, the intelligence coordination body established between our DFS and the Cuban DGI, should be sufficient to identify and address any threats to the Venezuelan government and people.
strings.MEX_VEN.35.a: Under the circumstances, I consider this a significant victory for the Veracruz alliance.
strings.MEX_VEN.36.t: Urgent Request for OCAE Support - Caracas
strings.MEX_VEN.36.desc:
Your Excellency,

At 22:30 yesterday, DIGEPOL, the intelligence service of our Venezuelan allies, notified the Cuban DGI and the Directorate of Federal Security through encrypted OCAE channels of a major breach in the city of Caracas. A DIGEPOL agent, recently recommended for termination based on several suspicious activities identified as we integrated Venezuelan intelligence into OCAE, fled the country with a significant portion of the agency's archives. The theft of these materials, focused on suspect military and police officials, political dissidents, and criminals in the nation's capital, has left DIGEPOL near blind in Caracas.

The traitorous agent is believed to have taken refuge in Iberia's Brazilian embassy. It is unclear if the theft was prearranged with the Iberians, or if the agent provided the information solely to facilitate defection. Either way, a hostile power has been given a significant opportunity to infiltrate and disrupt Venezuela.

I strongly recommend that all available resources be made available to support our Veracruz partner. DIGEPOL plans to conduct a series of arrests in three months' time to reestablish effective monitoring and preemption in Caracas. If these should fail, Venezuela's security situation may become unsalvageable.
strings.MEX_VEN.37.desc:
Below, in the shining abyss of the stage, the dramatic finale of the first act thundered, and the crescendo of violins seemed to try and outshout reality itself, hanging over Caracas. Meanwhile, a different atmosphere reigned in the shadowed private box. Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios sat in the velvet armchair, straight as a blade. His suit was impeccable, his parting ideal - a living embodiment of the era of President Alemán, when style was an extension of state discipline.

Beside him, DIGEPOL Director José Jesús Patiño González presented a sorry sight: his jacket was rumpled, his collar unbuttoned, and the man himself emanated the sour smell of fear and three days of insomnia. As the Cuban liaison began reading the intercept summary, the Venezuelan's head fell heavily onto his chest. He began to snore, cutting into the orchestra's score.

Barrios grimaced with disgust and lightly, but insistently, tapped the toe of his patent leather shoe against his colleague's leg. “Wake up, Señor, you are missing the climax,” he said in an icy tone. The Venezuelan jerked, rubbing his eyes. Barrios shook his head with a slight, almost sympathetic smirk. “You know, President Alemán used to say that a rumpled suit is a sign of a rumpled mind. For such an appearance at a briefing, he wouldn't have had you shot... he would have destroyed you with a look so withering you would have gladly tightened the noose around your own neck.”

The smile vanished from the Mexican's face as quickly as it had appeared. “Pull yourself together. Your service is bursting at the seams. You are trying to hold water in a sieve. You don't have the men for the whole city. Decide now: either we barricade ourselves in the Libertador government district, spitting on the outskirts, or we go into the slums to crush the infection in the bud, leaving the center naked. The choice is yours.”
strings.MEX_VEN.37.a: “We cannot lose the seat of power. Fortify Libertador.”
strings.MEX_VEN.37.b: “The enemy hides in the shadows of the outskirts. We go there.”
strings.MEX_VEN.38.desc:
The airstairs touched the scorching concrete of Maiquetía Airport, but instead of the usual motorcade and welcoming smiles, Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios was met only by the lonely figure of a junior adjutant with darting eyes. No Patiño, no honor guard. The air was thick with humidity and tension.

The messenger, stammering, conveyed the gist: the OCAE meeting was cancelled. The reason - “critical instability.” Worse, DIGEPOL was undergoing “deep internal restructuring.” Barrios knew this euphemism perfectly well. It meant a purge. The Venezuelans, having failed to uncover the Iberian network, had decided in a panic that their intelligence was either incompetent or infiltrated, and were now chopping off the head that ached.

The Captain slowly, with almost theatrical calm, took a thick cigar from his case. The lighter clicked. Barrios dragged deeply, blowing a stream of blue-grey smoke into the face of the harbinger of disaster, and his thoughts returned for a moment to the start of his career - to the dusty offices of Mexico City in '47, when the DFS was just being born from chaos and paranoia.

“Convey to your leadership,” he said, “that when we hunted enemies of the Revolution, we did not burn our own archives out of fear. What you have started is suicide. You are voluntarily gouging out your own eyes, hoping that way the Iberians won't find you.”

He turned sharply back to the stairs, not dignifying the adjutant with a parting glance. Venezuela had signed its own death warrant, and he had no intention of standing nearby when the executioner's axe fell.
strings.MEX_VEN.38.a: Empires crumble due to stupidity, not enemy strength.
strings.MEX_VEN.38.tt:
With the collapse of the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan internal security apparatus, in the event of a coup, the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan government will collapse like a house of cards.

Whether it be weeks, months, or years, the fall of our {mex_getflag} Veracruz ally is now a certainty.
strings.MEX_VEN.39.desc:
Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios snapped the folder stamped “Top Secret” shut and placed it on the table. In the air-conditioned cool of the DIGEPOL Director's office, the report read like a gripping spy novel with a happy ending. The summary was flawless: targeted arrests had mowed down the conspiracy's leadership, personnel rotation had decapitated disloyal garrisons, and the fake “rightist cells” created by intelligence had worked like flypaper, luring the most cautious traitors out of the shadows.

The Captain raised his eyes to the office's occupant. José Jesús Patiño González no longer resembled the rumpled clerk dozing at the opera. This time, he sat upright, radiating confidence. His suit was an exact replica of Barrios's own style, down to the width of the lapels and the shade of the tie.

The Mexican allowed himself a spare, approving smile.

“Brilliant work, Señor José. You have halted social dissolution and purged the rot from the system. Alemán would be proud of you,” Barrios stood and, walking around the desk, demonstratively adjusted the handkerchief in the Venezuelan's breast pocket. “And I see you have mastered my main lesson: order in the country begins with order in one's attire. An excellent choice of tailor.”

He paused, critically examining his colleague's face. “However, you will still have to work on the mustache. It lacks... let us say, the requisite luster and volume. But do not despair; Rome wasn't built in a day, either.”
strings.MEX_VEN.39.tt:
With the triumph of the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan internal security apparatus over dissident forces and their {ibr_getflag} backers, in the event of a coup, the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan government will prevail against those who seek to depose it.

The survival of our {mex_getflag} Veracruz ally will now be a certainty for many years to come.
strings.MEX_VEN.40.desc:
“Extra! Extra! President cuts rations for generals! Villalba against the Army!”

A newsboy's piercing cry sliced through the sleepy Caracas morning, making Don Ricardo grimace. The bulky man in an immaculate ivory linen suit stopped at the entrance to a bakery. He fastidiously dabbed the sweat on his fleshy neck with a starched handkerchief and, with a careless flick, sent a coin into the grubby palm.

The newspaper settled into his manicured hands. The headlines did not lie. Villalba, that quiet intellectual with a bull terrier's grip, had decided to commit political harakiri. Pay cuts, purges, restrictions on voting rights - a slap in the face to every man in uniform who considered himself a sacred guardian of the nation. “Jesus,” thought Ricardo, skimming the text. “What an idiot.”

The President wanted to subordinate bayonets to paragraphs of the constitution, to turn “saviors of the Fatherland” into boring civil servants. A noble goal for a political science textbook.

The businessman folded the paper and chuckled bitterly, watching an army truck drive by. “Good luck, Señor Presidente.” Villalba dreams of a “peaceful and stable state,” but the only thing he guarantees with these measures is that the coup that overthrows him will be carried out with perfect and frightening efficiency. Stability will come, without a doubt. But it will be ensured by the very people he has just humiliated.
strings.MEX_VEN.40.a: No one likes it when you reach into their pocket, especially men with rifles.
strings.MEX_VEN.41.t: Determined Reforms For a Determined Enemy
strings.MEX_VEN.41.desc:
“While such reforms are very important, caution must be exercised when trying to implement them,” said Luis I. Rodríguez, the Mexican Ambassador to Venezuela. He had come to speak with President Villalba and discuss the man's agenda over a pleasant lunch in Miraflores. Gabriel was officially Rodríguez's assistant, which allowed the DFS to have a voice at the meeting and keep up-to-date on Villalba's security.

Rodríguez took a sip from his drink before continuing, “The soldiers will be outraged when they catch word of the pay cuts and political restrictions. A silent group of officers still loyal to Pérez Jiménez within the ranks may cause a repeat of the 1948 coup if they aren't sated.”

A member of Villalba's staff walked up to the table and deposited a hefty stack of papers. From where Gabriel was sitting, they seemed to be stacks of orders and reform decrees in need of signatures. Villalba looked at Rodríguez and let out a small sigh, “Respectfully, Ambassador, while I agree with your government's concerns, do you have any other ideas on how I should go about things?”

Gabriel spoke up to give his suggestion, “You could water them down, place officers in key positions that would prevent a conspiracy from-”

Villalba shook his head, “Absolutely not. Have you heard of how many coups Venezuela has suffered in the past three decades? With such a determined enemy, Venezuela must have determined reforms. If that threatens my presidency, then so be it.”

A heavy silence sat in the air. Eventually, Rodríguez cleared his throat and steered the conversation away from the topic, but Gabriel couldn't keep himself from glancing at the soldiers posted at the door.
strings.MEX_VEN.41.a: After all, they had overheard the entire conversation.
strings.MEX_VEN.42.t: A Normal Stroll in the Park
strings.MEX_VEN.42.desc:
Gabriel and Rafael purchased breakfast at a street vendor in Chacaíto, took a seat on a bench, and began to chat, the two friends catching up on their personal lives over the past few days. From the outside, they looked like any old pair of friends passing time. In reality, while the two men were friends, Gabriel was a Mexican DFS agent, and Rafael worked for DIGEPOL. Between bites of their food, they glanced around the park. Apparently, former Perezjimenistas had picked up a habit of going on morning walks with unknown companions in these areas.

While Rafael was asking Gabriel about the answer to a crossword puzzle in his newspaper, Gabriel elbowed him and whispered, “On the other side of the fountain, passing by the street vendor, that's definitely Luis Felipe Llovera Páez. He's back in Caracas, apparently. You know who he's with? I don't recognize him.” Rafael shot a glance to where Gabriel had described, and while the stranger looked like another military man, Rafael didn't recognize him. Without a word, they threw out their half-eaten breakfasts and began to trail Llovera Páez.

Soon they could overhear the former exile's conversation, “It'll be a lightning, bloodless coup in Caracas, Villalba will be out of the way before he knows what hit him.”

Llovera Páez's mysterious buddy had a noticeable Spanish accent to his words, “And what about the rest of the country?”

Rafael and Gabriel had scribbled down everything they heard onto the backs of their newspapers and rushed back to the field headquarters. As they mapped out the notes they had obtained, Gabriel quickly began calling Miraflores. From where troops would be deployed to where supplies were stashed, the pair had stumbled upon a gold mine of information.
strings.MEX_VEN.42.a: And it wasn't even noon yet.
strings.MEX_VEN.43.desc:
The ringing of the phone startled Villalba and his wife awake. Rubbing his eyes as he fumbled around in the dark, Villalba reached over to his nightstand and brought the phonepiece to his ear. It was the director of DIGEPOL on the other end. “Sir, you need to come downstairs, the Minister of Defense and I are in the main room of Miraflores. It's urgent.” Villalba took a moment to register the words as his brain caught up to his body, before heading downstairs in his pajamas.

When he arrived in the room, Villalba's grogginess had mostly faded, and he felt exposed as he saw the sharply dressed men ready to greet him. The sky outside the windows was still pitch-black. As Villalba sat down, he asked, “So what's so important that you've woken me up at 3 in the morning?”

“As you are aware, DIGEPOL and the DFS have been monitoring the growth of a conspiracy within the army following you announcing your reforms. The conspiracy is set to launch their coup in just half an hour,” Villalba swore he felt the room lurch a bit at the news, “They seem to have been hoping they'd catch us off-guard, but we've already placed units and roadblocks on their planned paths, and set an alert for all loyal units to intercept and arrest conspirators on sight, wherever they are.”

Villalba's head was still spinning a bit from it all when the Minister of Defense handed him a coffee. Villalba stared at it blankly for a moment before asking, “Wait, that's good news. What is this coffee for, then?”

The DIGEPOL director laughed, “We figured you'd need something to wake you up. After all, you'll want to address the nation once we've bagged the conspirators, right?”

Villalba smiled, “Yes, yes, I guess I will. Thank you, gentlemen, and thank God for this wonderful news.”
strings.MEX_VEN.43.a: Now if you'll excuse me, I'll be heading back upstairs.
strings.MEX_VEN.44.desc:
Villalba sat in Ayacucho Hall, rereading his planned address over and over again, making occasional tweaks along the way. It wasn't something he did often, but on such a special and important occasion, he believed that his address had to be perfect.

Most presidents would stand before the nation and give a grand victory speech full of inflammatory, machista rhetoric after thwarting a coup. That wasn't what Venezuela needed right now. While he would denounce the armed forces, he'd place emphasis on the importance of his reforms and the need to implement them to their maximum effectiveness.

According to the clock hanging above him, it was around 7:00am. Only a minute or so later, a staffer told him he was on air. It was time to begin.

“Good morning, Venezuelans. A few short hours ago, a conspiracy within the armed forces attempted to overthrow our nation's government. They had attempted to storm the streets of Caracas, but fortunately were apprehended before any serious harm could be inflicted. These conspirators sought to use their place within the military to interfere into our democratic process, and overturn the will of the people. It is an abuse of their power of the highest order, and behavior that is incompatible with a stable, progressing, and democratic Venezuela.”

“That's why I call upon you, the people. It is only through your support that we can limit the army, to ensure that they will not interfere with politics. This conspiracy was launched in order to stop the reforms I had planned to limit the military's power within our politics, and it is only through the complete implementation of those reforms that we can safeguard our democracy from those who would seek to topple it.”
strings.MEX_VEN.44.a: Thank you, God bless you, and may God bless Venezuela.
strings.MEX_VEN.45.desc:
The last notes of the saxophone remained behind the heavy doors of the elite club in Chacaíto. Don Arturo, a well-known lawyer in Caracas, paid for his share of the tab and generously tipped the waitress, whose green eyes lit up with a wide smile. Adjusting his brown felt hat, he stepped into the cool night, anticipating the soft seat of his Cadillac. But instead of the silence of the pre-dawn city, he was met with a low, vibrating rumble that rattled the glass in the shop windows.

The street was clogged with iron. Canvas-covered trucks, APCs, and even light tanks crawled past, filling the air with blue-grey fumes. Soldiers in full gear roughly pushed indignant revelers back onto the sidewalk.

“What the devil?” - Arturo grabbed the sleeve of a running sergeant. “My driver is on the other side! What circus are you running here?”

The soldier, eyes wild with adrenaline, barked. “Emergency situation! An attack on the Fuerte Tiuna barracks in the south. All combat-ready units are on alert. Move back, Señor!”

The lawyer stepped back, trying to focus his drunken gaze. South. Fuerte Tiuna. That made sense. But then he looked at the road.

“Wait, son...” he muttered, pointing a shaky hand at the convoy of trucks rushing past. “If the fight is in the south, why are these vehicles heading north? Straight into the city center?”

“That's... reinforcements! Reserves!” shouted the soldier, already jumping onto the running board of a departing Dodge.

Arturo was left standing in a cloud of exhaust fumes. “Reinforcements” driving away from the battle? The alcohol in his blood said everything was fine, but his survival instinct, honed by years of legal intrigue, whispered that something very, very wrong was happening in Caracas tonight.
strings.MEX_VEN.45.a: The military's compass is clearly broken.
strings.MEX_VEN.46.desc:
“¡Señor Jóvito Villalba!”

This guttural shout, devoid of any respect, tore through the viscous silence of pre-dawn Miraflores like a gunshot. It was 4:30 AM. The Venezuelan Presidential Guard, stumbling from sleep, rushed to the main entrance, only to find there was nothing left to defend. The gates were wide open, the perimeter breached without a single shot fired-the cruel irony of “night maneuvers” that had led loyal garrisons south left the heart of power exposed.

In the vestibule, the guardsmen found themselves chest-to-chest with a forest of rifles from an entire infantry company. “Lower your weapons! No one gets hurt if you don't do anything stupid!” barked a rebel officer.

A solitary figure appeared at the top of the marble staircase. Villalba descended slowly. Slightly disheveled, without a tie, but in his invariable business suit, he tried to maintain a shred of presidential dignity in the face of an armed mob. Below, not dialogue, but an ultimatum awaited him. The coup leader, not even bothering with a salute, unfolded a crumpled sheet of paper and began reading a list of demands from an unknown General.

With each point, Villalba's face grew longer. It was not a political manifesto, but a surreal collection of absurdities canceling the constitution.

“I will not sign this paper, Captain,” the President cut him off quietly but firmly. “This is madness.”

The officer sighed with feigned sadness, tucking the paper into his pocket. “In that case, regrettably, you are under arrest, Señor. You will remain here, under supervision, until further notice.”

The heavy bolt of the main doors slammed into place with a clang. The sound of the cage snapping shut echoed off the high ceilings of the palace.
strings.MEX_VEN.47.t: How Did We Come to This?
strings.MEX_VEN.47.desc:
The VIP lounge of the Mexico City International Airport resembled a cold, modernist cavern. Endless rows of concrete columns stretched into the distance, reflected in the mirror-like sheen of the terrazzo floor. Beyond the panoramic windows, airliners with VARIG and SAESA logos roared into the sky, carrying happy people off to their quiet lives.

Villalba sat motionless, mechanically stroking the head of his sleeping child. The booming echo of dispatcher announcements mingled with his wife's quiet sobs, but to Jóvito, the noise sounded as if it were coming from underwater. One thought pounded in his head: “Where did I go wrong?”

Just twenty-four hours ago, he woke up in Miraflores as the President of a sovereign nation. And then reality crumbled: tanks under the windows, humiliating house arrest, and that slick colonel with the deportation order. “Leave immediately, for the sake of your children.” And here he is, in a foreign country. What about his parents? His wife's family? The ministers left in Caracas to be torn apart by wolves?

Leaden fatigue weighed on his shoulders, his eyes were closing, but Villalba's gaze accidentally caught the TV screen in the corner. Through the veil of exhaustion, the image of a news broadcast emerged: the new junta leader shaking hands with... the Iberian delegation. Smiles, embraces, promises of eternal friendship. He recognized the shit-eating grin of Matías Vega Guerra, the Iberian ambassador, which now looked down almost mockingly at him.

Villalba felt as if he'd been struck by lightning. Those two bastards... Franco and Salazar. They were in on it from the start. They knew every step and recognized the usurpers before the corpse of democracy had even gone cold. Villalba buried his face in his hands, feeling his impotent rage dissolve into a black, hopeless void.
strings.MEX_VEN.47.a: What can man do against such reckless hate?
strings.MEX_VEN.48.desc:
TOP SECRET // OCAE OPERATIONAL SUMMARY
SUBJECT: Domestic Reaction to the Essequibo Negotiations

1. President Rafael Caldera's diplomatic maneuvers are bearing fruit. His “silver tongue” and policy of appeasement are resonating strongly with the urban elite and business circles of Caracas. For them, the normalization of relations with Guyana and its backers is the key to Western markets and investments. Optimism reigns in the offices of the capital: peace promises to be profitable.

2. However, our agents are recording a critical rise in tension within “patriotic” organizations and the officer corps. What businessmen call pragmatism, nationalists brand as high treason. To them, the Essequibo is a sacred part of “Greater Venezuela,” amputated by colonialists.

3. Any compromise is perceived by these groups as capitulation to the “English usurpers.” The rhetoric at closed meetings is shifting from criticism to direct calls to “save the nation's honor” by force. We are witnessing the consolidation of radicals willing to set the country on fire just to keep the ink from drying on a peace treaty.

4. RECOMMENDATION: Initiate a heightened alert status for the residency in Caracas. Caldera's diplomatic triumph could become the detonator for an armed uprising.
strings.MEX_VEN.48.a: Peace for some is treason for others.
strings.MEX_VEN.49.desc:
“...For the greatness of a nation is measured not by the caliber of its guns, but by the firmness of its moral obligations,” Rafael Caldera's voice, amplified by the speakers, floated over the OAS assembly hall, hypnotizing the delegates. The President paused, sweeping the room with his gaze. “Next month in Port of Spain, we will meet with the leaders of Guyana and Canada to close the chapter of enmity forever. I thank our friends from Washington and, of course, our partners in the Veracruz Pact for their invaluable assistance in this dialogue.”

Caldera took a deep breath, preparing to deliver the decisive blow. “To prove to the world that our intentions are pure, I announce: tonight I will sign a decree for the full, indefinite withdrawal of the Venezuelan Armed Forces from the disputed borders.”

The hall exploded. Diplomats leaped from their seats, giving the peacemaker an ovation worthy of a rock star.

But the Mexican representative did not clap. His sharp gaze was fixed on the figures behind the President's back - the escort officers in dress uniform. He saw how the cheek of the colonel on the left twitched. How his knuckles turned white as they gripped the hilt of his ceremonial saber. In this sea of elation, the men in uniform stood like rocks against which the waves of applause broke. In their eyes, there was no thought of peace.

Only one word could be read there, written in the blood of their ambitions: “Betrayal.”
strings.MEX_VEN.49.a: He hears the applause, but he does not hear the knives being sharpened.
strings.MEX_VEN.50.t: Report on the Civil War in Venezuela
strings.MEX_VEN.50.desc:
DIRECCIÓN FEDERAL DE SEGURIDAD
ISSUE: Communist Uprising in Venezuela

5 hours ago, FALN-FLN troops in Venezuela seized control of Ciudad Bolívar and several other cities in the East, after the front declared a general uprising against the government. Sympathetic civilians have assisted the rebels in their offensive, allowing them to seize almost the entire east in a matter of hours. Despite the FALN intending a swift, large-scale revolution across the country, units in the west appear to have been pushed back to the Andes, allowing the central government to survive and reconsolidate. However, the uprising has escalated into a full-scale civil war.

The FALN has been a thorn in the side of the government since their formation in 1961 and formalization in the following year. Once considered marginal, the success of leftist movements in the Americas, along with civilian support from within, has emboldened them. Guerrilla operations also plague the countryside, and are expected to intensify as the war goes on.

It is imperative to our nation and the Veracruz Pact that we destroy the communist movement. Venezuela is a staunch ally of Mexico and a vital economic partner, holding the largest oil reserves in the world. Should they fall, our interests in the northern Andes and Caribbean will be greatly threatened, and our economy will undoubtedly suffer. Furthermore, the war must be ended quickly, as analysts predict that over time, the communists will only get stronger.

Very respectfully,
Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios
strings.MEX_VEN.53.desc:
The 'Papillón', officially just El Gran Café, was one of the more well-known hot spots in Sabana Grande. Situated outside a government building in Caracas, it sat beside an almost chaotic orchestra of buses, bikers and other heavy afternoon traffic hustling past the parade of policemen, street venders and well-to-do salarymen.

A DFS officer sat in a parked car outside the Papillón, the engine off, tinted windows up and a pen and pad gripped in steady hands. He had spied the labor union boss around 10 minutes prior, scrawling down their name around a dozen other names along with license plates numbers for any vehicles they arrived or left in. He would be sure to pass along the information to his liaison at the Interior Ministry later that day; after all, it wasn't paranoia if they really were out to get you.

The ignition was as far as the officer got. With the itinerary penciled down and the traffic letting up, he figured to not to linger. As turned the key, the block of Semtex strapped to the undercarriage, set by the UTC commandos, the FALN's urban wing, that had tracked him down, sent him into an early retirement and his vehicle straight up into the air, scattering smouldering pieces of both into the street and sidewalk.

No one else lost their life, no one else was even injured, even the damage to the front of the Papilion was minimal. A rare, clean kill by the FALN. It would not be the last one like it, but the others would not stay so clean for very long.
strings.MEX_VEN.54.t: Green to Red, On The Air
strings.MEX_VEN.54.desc:
The community radio station in Maracay was as plain and unassuming as the city it called home. Quaint, homey and, blissfully, far away from the fighting. La Mura was precisely as insistent as her name implied. 'The Wall' could be impatient, perhaps overly direct and not one to be told no. Yet strangely, blessed with a voice as gentle and warm as even the most ancient of abuelas. She used that voice to great effect; reading out messages from local families, job postings, weather updates and public service announcements.

That last part was what had been harrying her since the war broke out. As she sat in front of her microphone on her cigarette break, she eyed the missive on the desk in her recording booth with an increasingly jaded eye, the same one she had been receiving from the producer via his secretary for multiple weeks now.

Every now and again, she would get calls from people asking about the government in the ongoing crisis. They would ask whether the government was negotiating peace with the FALN or not, to which La Mura would read the typed-out statements urging some version of patience or unity or restraint. The prepared statements she received came in unmarked letters with no return addressed. Maybe she was thinking too much, but she suspected that they were coming from the Mexican Embassy in Caracas, even if she had no proof.

A hand-wave from her producer and the red light came on; They were about to go live, she dashed the cigarette, pulled on her headphones and readied herself for her show, prepared statements included. Someone had to read them out, didn't they?
strings.MEX_VEN.54.a: The lights above the recording studio door lit up: “NOW LIVE”
strings.MEX_VEN.55.desc:
Nino could not have been more normal. Tall and lean with a thin mustache, rounded glasses, and short black hair. His voice was high and whispy, his demeanor level-headed, and his mood subdued at nearly all times. Nino could not have been more normal, yet his nation was rapidly divorcing itself from any sort of normalcy by the day.

He had been filling out the necessary forms at a law office in Barquisimeto, walls lined with certificates and dusty photos of past mayors sharing handshakes with foreign diplomats. As a lawyer, he was used to red tape like this, yet that word, 'red', wasted little time in gaining a very different meaning in Venezuela. For weeks now, families from all over the city had come, gone, and would likely continue to do so for weeks to come, all inquiring how to apply for Mexican residency. 'Fleeing' was not a word people used; 'Escaping' was an absurd idea; 'Refugee' was too insulting to ponder. 'Just in case' was the word people had settled on. No one needed to know the reason behind it anymore; it was known.

When Nino was done with the paperwork, he headed straight to the consular window he knew would review them the fastest. Blissfully, respectfully, they did not ask why, but Nino knew all he needed to. With the land routes along the Colombian border no longer safe to travel since La Violencia and the Dutch forcing illegal refugees back over the border from the shores of Curaçao and Aruba, seeking sanctuary within the Veracruz Pact nations was the only legitimate way to escape the civil war worth considering.

As he walked out the front door to his car, Nino could hear the distant sounds of the Turbio River, something that used to give him calm. Now? He couldn't tell what was louder, the rushing of the Turbio or the screams of Little Andrés in the hospital burn ward, burned shin to scalp from the bombing last month, dead at 14, another so-called 'martyr' of the UTC's revolution.
strings.MEX_VEN.55.a: Whatever future there was in Mexico, if there was any, was for him to find out, but not to know.
strings.MEX_VEN.56.t: Green to Red, Over the Road
strings.MEX_VEN.56.desc:
One did not need to be told where the border road near Santa Elena de Uairén led to, for even the most uneducated foreigner could not fail to recognize the Amazon rainforest, the greater breadth of which lay further on beyond the borderline into northern Brazil. Two paper cups of cheap coffee sat on the hood of a rusty yellow Chevrolet truck, situated between a Venezuelan intelligence captain and an agent of the Mexican DFS who sat next to each other.

The idle engine hummed underneath them, the headlights beaming into the deep, thick jungle brush as they sat and drank. There was no identifiable uniform between either of them, just plain clothes for a plain pair of people with a pair of plain goals. There was no introduction needed, they did not shake hands. Between when they arrived and when they would leave, there would not be a word said between them.

The envelopes said everything, as they were the reason for their arrival. One contained the names of supply couriers collaborating with the UTC guerrillas in the interior, backing the FALN's war effort. The other contained the requests for political asylum, thoroughly unofficial from the lack of a civil seal or government letterhead, all listed for individuals with the same last name, including that of the intelligence captain.

The DFS federale received his letter, the intel captain received his. They finished up their coffee before setting off on their separate ways, taking a brief moment to enjoy the local flora and fauna.
strings.MEX_VEN.56.a: You take what peace you can find in a place like this.
strings.MEX_VEN.57.t: Green to Red, Bad to Worse
strings.MEX_VEN.57.desc:
The records were a literal litany of the history of the country that was now to be irrevocably changed. The folders contained baptism records from the early 60s, marriage papers from the 50s, old passports from the 40s, and even further back, all carried by the growing line of people that had formed outside the Mexican consulate since before sunrise. This was the vision of the FALN victory in Venezuela, of pleading eyes, of shaking hands, of racing hearts.

The consulate staff, to their credit, was utterly devoted around the clock to clearing as many people for emigration to Mexico as they could. They stamped documents, filed requests and approved residency as quickly as their system, however much of it still officially existed, could allow.

Mexico was no stranger to conflict and neither was Venezuela. They both had seen conflicts like this, just not on their own soil. The men and women of the Mexican consulate did not dare lecture anyone and didn't ask for explanations. This was cruelty that the Venezuelan people were enduring, and the stall would do as much as they could to alleviate it.

Yet for all their efficiency and tact, they could only work so quickly for the number of people hoping to flee the Reds and whatever fate they had in store for them. Outside the consulate, the heat was building, the line was growing, and no one was leaving. Inside the consulate walls, the staff could barely hear their own voices, burying their heads in a sea of paper and ink while line after line of people begged for mercy, for any chance for a way out, for any hope of a future away from the one that awaited them on the next sunrise.
strings.MEX_VEN.57.a: The trials of Venezuelans are only just beginning.
strings.MEX_VEN.58.t: Green to Red, Business as Usual
strings.MEX_VEN.58.desc:
The clatter of the filing cabinet drawer was the sound of the last unofficial act of the DFS on the ground in the Venezuelan theater, or at least that concerning the Civil War. The files within contained lists of names, personal notes, and observations on key persons of interest that were never formally filed, yet the Venezuelan government was sure to use them for the future. The FALN and UTC may have been driven into the jungle, but keeping tabs on their former allies hiding in the crowd was a worthwhile endeavor. If they were to return to civilian life, that could be acceptable. If not, something more acceptable could be arranged.

The official statement from Mexico City was nothing short of dignified, if sounding a little detached. The defeat of the Communist insurgency was a real victory for the Veracruz Pact, but you almost wouldn't know that a principal ally of the VP just went through a harrowing civil war. No one along the Caribbean wanted to admit that Venezuela almost went the way of Castro, but who would after everything they had worked so hard to build, free from corrosive influences abroad?

The DFS agent left his temporary office with nothing but the clothes on his back, a doctored ID in his pocket, and a small, black suitcase. As he made his way outside, the air in Caracas was strangely in tune with the Mexican statement. Traffic ebbed and flowed like water in a stream, street vendors shouted while dogs barked on sloped sidewalks. No smoke, no fire, not anymore.

The agent ducked into the back of a taxi he had hailed, not even bothering to look back through the rear window. He would be on the first charter flight back to Mexico City and another quick taxi back to his townhome in Colonia Juárez. There was no report left to deliver, nothing else left to catalog. It was Venezuela who remained, she and her ever-enduring people.
strings.MEX_VEN.58.a: The sun would soon set on Lake Maracaibo, with many cool, quiet nights to follow.
strings.MEX_VEN.59.t: One Ant of the Colony Squashed
strings.MEX_VEN.59.desc:
A cell of Bolivarian military conspirators sat in an empty warehouse outside Caracas. The group was sorting through newly-delivered crates of rifles and intelligence briefings with their Iberian contact. “Coming all the way from Madrid, must be the best.”

The contact with a heavy Castilian lisp responded. “Make thure everyone ith up to date. Can't have anything go wrong thith deep into the plan.”

In the corner of the warehouse a small box television played the nightly news. Images showed President Caldera signing the Port of Spain Accords, flanked by the Guyanese President, {guy_getleader}, and the Canadian Prime Minister, {can_getleader}. One of the conspirators watching lashed out at the screen. “Just imagine, by daybreak that cocksucker will be wishing he never surrendered to the Guyanese bastards, he's a damn shame to Venezuela.”

A crack, the conspirators grabbed their new Iberian rifles. A combination of DIGEPOL agents and National Guard soldiers burst into the warehouse to arrest the group. When the conspirators attempted to fire, a grave expression quickly took their faces, these new guns weren't real, they'd been duped.

The Iberian, or so they had thought, dropped the lisp to speak in the clear Mexican accent of a DFS agent. “Drop them, otherwise you'll be killed.” The DIGEPOL agents moved in to apprehend the conspirators and haul them out of the warehouse.

As the Mexican was leading the last one out, the conspirators' radio, left sitting on the table, crackled with Moncada Vidal's voice. “My loyal soldiers, we now stand at the moment of national liberation. All who believe in our nation, and in the strength of our men to lead it are called! Any who stand against us, soldier or civilian, is an enemy that will be dealt with as enemies are! Forward!.”
strings.MEX_VEN.60.t: Rather Die Standing, Then Live Kneeling
strings.MEX_VEN.60.desc:
As President Caldera's plane descended upon Caracas, all that could be seen were rivers of people, with a sprinkle of armored vehicles, filling what were once the city's streets. As soon as the plane landed, Caldera nearly jumped right onto the tarmac and was ushered into the DIGEPOL director's car by the sharply-dressed man himself. While the car sped toward the control tower, the director briefed the President.

“Luckily, Your Excellency, the majority of the attack was thwarted from our infiltration, several conspirators throughout the military have already been arrested. However, their leader, Moncada Vidal, did get away with his detachment and has seized the White Palace. He's rallying for a revolt because of the Essequibo resolution.”

“That rat Moncada Vidal... just get me to the people, they need to hear from me.” The car arrived at the tower and the entire detail rushed inside. From inside, Caldera was patched through to national radio to address the nation.

“People of Venezuela, this is President Caldera, I'm alive and well. The rebels led by Lieutenant Colonel Moncada Vidal have seized the White Palace. They have struck in the heart of Caracas using an idea of national pride to hide their oppressive goals.”

Caldera paused to steady his voice, continuing. “I call on all the people of Venezuela, to rise up. No matter who you are or where you are at, we must fight the threat to our revolution and democracy. The only way to beat the putschists is a united front of the people. A people who love liberty will, when all is done, be free.”

Shortly after the broadcast had ended a plume of smoke began rising from Urdaneta Avenue. The people not only listened to their President's call, but answered it.
strings.MEX_VEN.60.a: The battle for Caracas had begun.
strings.MEX_VEN.61.desc:
Venezuelan nationals working in the Mexican embassy flowed into the streets of Caracas. Within the crowd, “Miguel” The Clerk joined the revelry, maintaining the cover that the DFS so scrupulously demanded of him, all being absorbed into the swelling crowd following President Rafael Caldera's escort. The crowd waved Venezuelan flags and sang the anthem. “¡Gritemos con brío: Muera la opresión!”

The convoy passed burning military trucks and abandoned armored vehicles, remnants of Moncada Vidal's coup, as they approached Miraflores Palace. President Rafael Caldera emerged from the convoy, with a megaphone, addressing the crowd. “From the deepest of my heart I extend my thanks, a thanks to all of you that have defended Venezuela's democracy, and her future.”

The crowd occupied all of central Caracas and roared in cheers for Caldera as he continued. “The vast majority of the conspirators in this plot have already been apprehended. All of these men will face trial with their full legal rights. No matter how much they claimed otherwise, this country's strength is its constitution and its people. Just because they would break it against us, doesn't give us cause to break it against them.”

The crowd erupted into applause as Caldera handed the megaphone off as he was escorted away by security. Miguel cracked a slight smile, joining the Venezuelans now signing the anthem once again. “Gloria al bravo pueblo, que el yugo lanzo, la ley respetando, la virtud y honor...” and he put greater emphasis at the start of the new verse...
strings.MEX_VEN.62.desc:
One last wave to the cameras, and Caldera was on the plane. He took his seat, breathing a sigh of relief. Despite everything, the negotiations had been a success. Another foreign-policy feather for his presidential cap. In a few minutes, he would leave Trinidad behind and return to his real work. Just as he closed his eyes to catch some much-needed sleep, a sweating, pale-faced aide rushed onto the plane.

“Sir, we got word-” stammered an aide, hardly more than a boy.

“Slow down, son,” Caldera said.

“Sorry,” the aide swallowed. “Well, we called to make sure the troops near the Guyanese border got the order to stand down...” The aide gave Caldera a nervous glance. “We can't get in touch with them, sir. Any of them. And not just at the border. Whole sections of the military aren't responding.”

“Which ones?” Caldera asked. Maybe only a few had backstabbed him, but the aide kept rattling off names, each one slamming into him like a punch to the gut. Generals. Sergeants. Every rank had betrayed him, but rank hardly mattered in these times of shifting loyalties. And between all of them, he could still piece together one common denominator.

“Moncada Vidal's people... This is his move.” Caldera stood, rattling out his own set of orders. “Get in touch with Air Force Headquarters. Tell them to assume all ground forces are compromised.” He turned to his stable of aides, all of whom were listening intently. “Call the Mexican embassy, I need to know what's happening in Caracas.”

Leaving them to their tasks, Caldera made for the cockpit. If he could beat them to the presidential palace and rally enough loyal troops to defend the capital, he might have a chance. He leaned over the pilot's chair.
strings.MEX_VEN.63.desc:
Caldera felt a slight bit of turbulence as the plane continued its steady path toward Caracas. He looked outside to see bright bursts of flame burning throughout the city and masses of people in the streets. Moncada Vidal's attempted coup had created a roiling air of discontent as the people turned against him and his Iberian masters. Once he could land at La Carlota Air Base, then he could help lead his people to final victory.

Another jolt, but this time it was worse than mere turbulence. González, a young and particularly headstrong policy aide, looked outside the opposite window. “Your Excellency, it's anti-aircraft fire!”

Caldera's eyes went wide. If Moncada Vidal's forces were able to take control of La Carlota, then it meant a good portion of the military infrastructure of Venezuela was compromised. He took a look at the staff on the plane with him, their mouths pursed, and knew that they had come to the same conclusion. As he felt the plane alter course, a staffer brought him an encrypted comms system, explaining that the loyalist leadership cadre was trying to contact him.

“Señor Rafael, are you ready to land? We need your support, the situation down here worsens by the minute.” Caldera couldn't tell whose voice it was over the crackling line, but Caldera believed it was his Minister of Defense, Martín García Villasmil.

Caldera's voice trembled. “There isn't a secure place where the plane can land. But I implore you to hold out until we can retake La Carlota, then we will return.”

As he spoke the words, Caldera looked out the window and knew that it was a lie. This moment, in a plane wracked by anti-aircraft fire flying over a burning capital, would be seared into his brain as the last sight of his country he would ever see. He couldn't muster the strength to admit that he failed, to implore his loyalists to flee across the border to make it to Mexico.
strings.MEX_VEN.63.a: Once verbose, Caldera found that he had not the words.
strings.MEX_VEN.64.desc:
Rafael Caldera couldn't help but think of the plane he was in as his hearse. This was the plane that had taken him to Venezuela, the plane that showed him his capital awash in flame, the plane that had rocked back and forth against an old air-defense explosive shell that let him know that he was never coming back. While no official request had come, Caldera knew it was only a matter of time before he had to leave Trinidad, and so he decided to make it easy for the island and depart for his permanent asylum in Mexico City.

The skies were smooth, but no one felt at ease. Many could barely compose themselves, this final admission of defeat cut through any remaining illusions. They were going to a foreign land, to live and die on unfamiliar soil. They might return, but it would never be by their own hands. They had tried that already and had failed.

Caldera saw González, head in his hands, and walked over to him. “González, was it? How are you doing? Did your family make it to an embassy?”

González looked dazed for a second, as if his brain struggled to form any sort of coherent thought. “I...don't know, Your Excellency. I haven't heard a word from them. I've been praying every night, twice even when I heard that Moncada Vidal's forces were gunning down protesters in the streets and kicking down the doors of suspected loyalists.”

Caldera nearly choked. The legacy of his quest for peace was blood in the streets that ran like rivers. The people who had believed in him were being hunted down by Moncada Vidal's forces. His desires for peace had burned in the fires of war. Just like González, his mind went to others who were in Venezuela. How many of them would have reached safety, finding an embassy or crossing the border? How many faces would he see in Mexico City, and how many lives would end dumped into a mass grave, known only to the fascists and the worms?
strings.MEX_VEN.64.a: The dead, buried in graves. The living, buried in guilt.
strings.MEX_VEN.65.t: Green to Red, Red to Black
strings.MEX_VEN.65.desc:
From the Office of the Mexican Embassy in Caracas, Venezuela.
To the Office of External Relations of Mexico in Mexico City, Mexico.

- With the progression of the Venezuelan war not going in the government's favor, Caracas has ceded authority of the government to a military junta led by General Pablo Antonio Flores following a bloodless coup.

- Position of the military regime is entrenched, with General Flores backed by large portions of the Venezuelan military. Elections have been suspended for the duration of the conflict. Many are worried about the possibility this will continue even with the FALN defeated.

- Under the current conditions, it is difficult to recommend continued support as has been up to now. But with the civil war still raging, Venezuela and her people are still in need of support from the Veracruz Pact.

- Mexico City would be within legal rights via international law to justify Venezuela's expulsion from the VP, but this is to be avoided if possible. It is advisable that material aid to Venezuela should continue for the duration, with the threat of expulsion to be used as leverage to ensure the return of democratic processes on the eventual defeat of UTC/FALN forces.
strings.MEX_VEN.65.a: Maintain intel and material support while quieting discussion in the Veracruz Forum.
strings.MEX_VEN.65.b: Work to prop up the image of Flores' Junta and send further aid to the war effort.
strings.MEX_VEN.65.c: Allow the Veracruz Forum to condemn the Junta and cease aid until democracy is restored.
